items.body:
Tomorrowland is bringing its CORE concept to Australia for the first time — and tickets are already gone.

Set to take over The Nursery at Flemington Racecourse, Melbourne, on 28 November, the inaugural CORE Melbourne will bring together international electronic heavyweights and homegrown talent for a day of house, techno, and underground sounds.

The sold-out Australian debut marks another milestone in CORE’s international expansion. Having staged editions across Europe, the Americas, and Asia, Melbourne brings the Tomorrowland concept to its fifth continent and its furthest destination from home yet.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CORE (@core.world)

Leading the lineup are Honey Dijon, Mall Grab, Effy, Moodymann, TSHA, Dino Lenny, Daria Kolosova, and Kobosil. Mall Grab and Effy will join forces for a special back-to-back set, while Melbourne selectors Jennifer Loveless and Jnett are also part of the bill.

Rounding out the lineup are fumi, Hannah D, Hitmiløw, Lola Voss b2b Billy Currie, and Noise Mafia b2b Peterblue.

CORE Melbourne will feature multiple stages, including the return of the Mano stage. Making only its second appearance at a CORE festival following its debut in Los Angeles, the stage will focus on underground sounds with sets from Daria Kolosova, fumi, and Colombian artists Noise Mafia b2b Peterblue.

The event will also bring CORE's signature visual world to The Nursery, a green open-air space within Flemington Racecourse. The concept is known for combining electronic music with nature-inspired staging, technology, and immersive visual storytelling.

CORE Melbourne is organised by Collective Minds and Framed Agency. The festival is also presented in partnership with Australian non-profit ticketing platform Humanitix, which donates its profits from booking fees to charitable initiatives, including education programmes for disadvantaged children.

items.body:
After bringing their global showcase across Asia, NEXZ finally made their way to Singapore last month. The Capitol Theatre stop followed shows in Taipei, Hong Kong, and Bangkok, giving TOMOYA, YU, HARU, SO GEON, SEITA, HYUI, and YUKI another chance to meet NEX2Y across the region — and, as the members tell Bandwagon, discover just how much energy they draw from performing in front of their fans.

The showcase arrived during a packed chapter for NEXZ. Fresh from their first-ever Japan arena tour, the group released their third Japanese EP, Hellmate, a four-track project spanning the title track, 'Hands up, Yo!', 'Can’t hide', and a Japanese version of 'Mmchk'. Across the record, NEXZ move between hip-hop, rock, and R&B while holding onto the playful confidence and individuality at the heart of their music.

Following their Singapore show, Bandwagon caught up with NEXZ to talk about finding their identity across different sounds, the Hellmate parts they wish were theirs, eating their way through Asia, and how hearing NEX2Y sing along has inspired them to get even more involved in making their own music.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

You've just wrapped up your first arena tour and your global showcase across Asia. What's one thing you've learned about yourselves as performers that you didn't know before stepping onto this tour?

HYUI: We held our global showcase and had the chance to visit many different places and meet so many NEX2Y. Through that experience, we realised once again that while we spend a lot of time practising, performing, and dancing, nothing makes us happier or gives us more energy than performing in front of NEX2Y, our fans.

Congratulations on your third EP, Hellmate! The EP moves between hip-hop, rock, and R&B. As NEXZ continues to experiment with different sounds, what do you think is the one thing that always makes a song feel unmistakably "NEXZ"?

HARU: NEXZ’s music covers a wide range of genres, but no matter what kind of song it is, each one really brings out the unique qualities of our voices. Whatever the genre, we hope that when you hear our music, you’ll immediately think, “This is NEXZ!” So please give all of our songs lots of love and listen to them!

The title track 'Hellmate' is built around encouraging people to stay true to themselves regardless of what society says. Was there a moment during the making of this EP where you felt that message reflected your own journey as a group?

SEITA: As we practised the performance, performed the song on stage, and filmed the music video, we felt that there were many ways in which 'Hellmate' reflected our own journey as NEXZ.

One thing that especially stood out to us is that, as we continue our activities as NEXZ, we often talk about wanting to show everyone who supports us, including all of our fans, our own unique colour and musical identity. In that sense, the idea of showing and sharing our own colour really connects with the lyrics of 'Hellmate'.

If each member had to recommend just one track from Hellmate to a first-time listener, which song would you pick and why?

SO GEON: I'd like to recommend 'Can’t hide'. This is our first time singing a heartbreak song, and I think you’ll get to hear a new side of each member through our sweet vocals. The lyrics also really hit you in the heart, so we hope you’ll give it a listen!

Is there another member's killing part on Hellmate that made you think, "I wish that was mine"? Show us your version!

YUKI: There’s a part I really love in 'Hands up, Yo!' It’s SEITA’s part where he says, “Right, bro?” We all love that part so much and imitate it all the time. Let me do my version! TOMOYA, give me your hand. “Right, bro?” Bro!

items.body:
Demon Hunter has filed a trademark lawsuit against Netflix over the name of its hit animated film KPop Demon Hunters.

Filed on 18 August by Hyde Lane, the company behind the Seattle Christian metal band, the complaint names Netflix Studios and concert promoter AEG Presents. Demon Hunter alleges that the success and expansion of KPop Demon Hunters across music, merchandise, and live entertainment have created “substantial confusion” among consumers.

The band has been active for 25 years and registered the “Demon Hunter” trademark for recorded music and merchandise in 2022. It has also applied for trademark protection covering live music.

According to the lawsuit, one fan reportedly spent US$500 on tickets to a Demon Hunter concert in Albany, New York, believing they were purchasing tickets to a child-friendly KPop Demon Hunters show. The complaint also cited a television producer who mistakenly contacted the band’s management believing it was connected to the Netflix property, as well as social media users incorrectly tagging the group in posts about the film.

Demon Hunter argues that Netflix’s plans for live performances further increase the overlap between the two brands. The band is asking the court to prevent Netflix from using the KPop Demon Hunters name in connection with recorded music, live performances, and merchandise, while also seeking unspecified damages.

Netflix has separately registered “KPop Demon Hunters” as a trademark for several merchandise categories, with further applications pending.

Released in 2025, KPop Demon Hunters follows fictional K-pop trio HUNTR/X as they balance their careers as pop stars with fighting demons. The film has since become Netflix’s most-watched original title, while its soundtrack and related music have also become major hits.

The film went on to win Best Animated Film and Best Original Song for 'Golden' at both the Golden Globes and Academy Awards. A sequel has also been confirmed, while Netflix is reportedly considering further projects including a television series and stage musical.

A global KPop Demon Hunters live tour is expected to begin in 2027.

items.body:
Andrea Bocelli is heading back to Indonesia for two special performances celebrating three decades of his landmark album Romanza.

Presented by Bank SMBC Indonesia and BNI, Andrea Bocelli Romanza 30th Anniversary World Tour Indonesia: Two Wonders, One Voice will take place on 31 October at Borobudur Temple in Magelang, followed by a second concert on 3 November at Jakarta International Expo (JIExpo) Kemayoran in Jakarta.

According to organisers, the shows will be Bocelli's only public performances in Southeast Asia this year. The two concerts will bring the Italian tenor's music to two distinctly different settings, from the historic surroundings of Borobudur to the heart of Jakarta.

The anniversary tour commemorates 30 years of Romanza, the album that became a defining release in Bocelli's career and introduced listeners around the world to songs including 'Con Te Partirò'.

The Borobudur show is also set to extend beyond the concert itself. Ticket holders will receive access to a cultural village showcasing the heritage, traditions, and local character of Magelang and Central Java. Organisers envision the performance as a cultural experience in the vein of Bocelli's appearances at historic sites around the world, including the Pyramids of Giza, the Acropolis, and the Vatican.

“It is truly an honour to bring a world-class maestro like Andrea Bocelli to Indonesia,” said Shoemaker Studios founder Prajna Murdaya. “Romanza concert is especially meaningful as it brings this timeless artistry to two remarkable settings, Borobudur and Jakarta, creating moments audiences can cherish long after the music ends.”

Tickets are priced from IDR 1,000,000, with premium categories going above IDR 15,000,000. Selected top-tier categories will also include access to an exclusive pre-event VIP lounge.

A 72-hour presale for Jenius and BNI debit and credit cardholders will begin on 21 August at 1 PM WIB and run until 24 August at 1 PM WIB, with discounts of up to 20%. Tickets will be available exclusively via Tiket.com during the presale. Travel bundles combining concert tickets, transportation, and hotel stays will also be offered through the platform. items.body:
ONE OR EIGHT are celebrating their anniversary with new music — and a special gift for the fans who have been with them along the way.

The eight-member group released their new English-language ballad 'INVINCIBLE', marking the second single from their forthcoming debut EP, EN-GÏNE (slated for release on 16 September). The track follows July's 'YANKEE SQUAT'.

Dedicated to their fandom, 1DERZ, 'INVINCIBLE' centres on the connection ONE OR EIGHT have built with their fans since their debut. With lyrics including “We're never alone” and “With you I'm invincible”, the track serves as a message of gratitude to those who have supported the group through their journey so far.

'INVINCIBLE' was produced by TK (UP), with songwriting credits from Edwin Honoret (PRETTYMUCH), BBY NABE, and Jordan Dennis. The latter collaborators have previously worked on ONE OR EIGHT tracks including 'TOKYO DRIFT' and 'YANKEE SQUAT'.

Its title combines the Japanese word "EN" (縁), referring to connection or fate, with "GENE". According to the group, the project represents a new driving force created through the relationships between its eight members and their fans around the world.

Following their mini-album GATHER, EN-GÏNE will explore the uncertainty, pressure, and self-doubt that come with pursuing dreams on a global stage, as well as the courage that can come from having others by your side.

Alongside the new release, ONE OR EIGHT have also announced ONE OR EIGHT Special SHOW CASE 2026 in ASIA -V8-, which will bring the group to three Southeast Asian cities this October.

ONE OR EIGHT Special SHOW CASE 2026 in ASIA -V8-

21 October — Singapore

23 October — Manila

25 October — Bangkok

Further ticketing and venue details will be announced soon.

items.body:
Siiry Debuts As A Producer With Fuzzy Melancholic Dance Pop Single 'Deja Vu'

20 August 2026

After rising as a DJ through this decade, Hyderabad's Siiry assumes the role of a producer with her debut single 'Deja Vu'.

Though packing a bouncy groove that gets the body moving like her efforts on the dancefloor, Siiry chooses an entirely different aim with the track as she creates "an ode to nostalgia — a love letter to everything that feels familiar and comfortable, including the patterns - both good and bad - that we find ourselves returning to."

Consequently, the song comes with the fuzzy textures and detuned keys that evoke that melancholic yearning-for-past feeling very dominantly found in lo-fi house, except delivered over a more dynamic interplay of drums and bass. Alongside the synth interludes, Siiry buries her voice in echoey washes till it just about switches from being the central songwriting to an ambient layer. All of it serves a single emotional purpose, and that in itself showcases surprising musical maturity, especially for a debut production.

Watch the music video for 'Deja Vu' below and follow Siiry for more information.

items.body: Over the course of a month-long bicycle journey across southern and central Thailand, H. Flora accumulated a personal archive of nocturnal field recordings. These recordings became the basis for two interconnected releases, each approaching the same ecosystems from a different perspective. Anthropause presents the material in its raw form: rainforests alive with gibbons, amphibian choirs, Tokay geckos, bats and insects captured during the hours when human activity had receded to its minimum. Noumenon takes those same recordings as its starting point, reshaping them through modular synthesis, electronic processing and improvisation into a “naturel-concrète” ecosystem. The relationship between the albums never feels schematic. Anthropause already demonstrates a careful compositional ear. Each lengthy piece unfolds episodically through changing densities and acoustic perspectives rather than functioning as a documentary collage. Different species occupy distinct spatial registers, creating a strong sense of internal organisation without any intervention beyond careful listening and recording. H. Flora repeatedly resists the temptation to isolate individual sounds, allowing the rainforest to remain a collective acoustic environment whose complexity exceeds immediate human understanding. That sense of immersion carries naturally into Noumenon. Here the field recordings dissolve into modular drones, fractured rhythms and densely layered electronic textures whose origins are often impossible to identify. Animal calls become synthetic oscillations before gradually revealing their biological source; electronic gestures acquire the behaviour of insects or amphibians. Nature and technology enter into a continuous exchange, with the album always remaining profoundly organic. What ultimately distinguishes these releases is the absence of ecological sentimentality. H. Flora is not constructing a fantasy of untouched wilderness, nor imagining a world cleansed of humanity. His recordings repeatedly acknowledge how difficult it has become to find moments free from anthropogenic noise, while Noumenon accepts that any attempt to imagine a post-human ecosystem remains speculative. Heard in parallel, the two albums also begin to unsettle the listener’s assumptions about sound itself. The raw recordings of Anthropause, with their hissing rainforests, reveal the mechanics of nature through high frequencies, rhythmic pulses, amphibian loops and electronic-sounding timbres, while Noumenon demonstrates how organic modular synthesis and digital processing can become when they remain attentive to those same acoustic behaviours. The boundary between documentation and invention becomes increasingly porous, exposing just how strange and sonically complex the natural world already is. Personally — and somewhat ironically — I found that, at times, Noumenon adhered more faithfully to my own imagined soundscape of a rainforest in Thailand. For this armchair traveller, H. Flora’s “Nocturnal Fantasias” may even feel more authentic than the ambience documented on Anthropause. Of course, I am exaggerating here, but this also goes to show how difficult it can be to leave one’s own expectations behind, even when embarking remotely on a sonic expedition. Across the two albums, bioacoustics and electroacoustic composition become part of the same exploratory process, beginning with the act of listening and following wherever the sounds happen to lead. Taking us on his travels, H. Flora kindly answered a few questions via email elaborating on the production process. The two releases, Anthropause and Noumenon, feel like complementary perspectives on the same material. One presents the rainforest as recorded, while the other imagines how these ecosystems might evolve in the prolonged absence of humanity. At what point did you realise that the project needed to exist in these two parallel forms rather than as a single album? Well, it was more of a fluid process than a decision. When I scanned through the original material to see what I could find and did some cutting around parts where there was subtle human activity, I realised again how challenging it was to capture sonic moments in which those sounds could really be perceived in an isolated, pure form. So, by making chops here and there, I started to extract parts that I really liked and began playing around with them. It just came naturally over time from this initial idea of capturing the sonic footprint of the non-human world, and I felt it could be extended by building something on top of that attempt. More in the sense that I could create my own individual idea of a possible version of the anthropause. The title Anthropause refers to the idea of a temporary withdrawal of human activity from the environment. During your nocturnal recordings across Thailand, were you trying to document moments where nature seemed to reclaim the acoustic foreground, or was the album also a reflection on the impossibility of ever fully removing the human presence from contemporary ecosystems? I mean, for me it is more an excercise to record in nature. It is a way to expand my own senses and to visualize how beautiful and unique it can be to get yourself into this multilayered, complex non-human world of communication and sonic order and chaos. Therefore, I need to search sometimes for the acoustic space on which i want to focus to get into this certain sphere of perception. The partly highly contrasting sounds created by humans and the quantitatively presence, its effects on the territorial behaviour of animals and therefore, among other things, on the sonic landscapes is sure something which can not be dismissed overall while recording. also myself, I am part of this ambivalent relation. we are all. So I didn’t really want to reduce the framework of these pieces on a imagination, where humankind finally vanished for its sinful, destructive nature of being and an acoustic domesticity being finally claimed again by the so called natural world and so on. I found it more fitting to see and understand it as a kind of Noumenon, something that can be measured from a certain perspective and that one has a responsibility to react to, but which, on the other hand, cannot really be perceived in its entirety; something one cannot fully understand in all its dimensions, and something that is not perceptible solely through a human understanding of things. The earthly sphere and its ecosystem have their own complex “logic”, with or without our presence. And it is also the case that the sonic stage should be allowed to belong to someone else for a change.. You spent a month travelling through Thailand by bicycle, often recording after 10 p.m. or before dawn to minimise human interference. How did those long periods of isolated listening change your relationship with environmental sound? Were there particular encounters—whether the gibbons of Phang Nga, the amphibian choirs, the Tokay geckos, or the cave-dwelling bat colonies—that fundamentally altered your understanding of these ecosystems? It was more like a last-minute trip and, in general, when I travel nowadays, I’m not really well prepared and I do it without much planning. So basically, I had absolutely no idea what to expect when I arrived there. I had got these new clip-on microphones beforehand, and my intention was to get familiar with them, play around and experiment a bit. But I quickly noticed after arriving that there was a huge sonic landscape to explore. I remember that somewhere on the coast I started making my first recordings at night, and this one animal was very close to me and had this strange, distinctive sound. So the next morning I asked some people around the bungalows and played them my recording. It was a tokay gecko, and for the locals it was more than familiar. They were giggling—it’s a well-known guy there. This kind of thing happened to me many times. I remember sitting in a small roadside restaurant at night in Khao Sok National Park and having a lot of fun talking with the owners. Then this frog began to croak. I pointed towards the sound and they immediately responded that it was the “bullfrog”, because it blows up its cheeks in order to make the sounds it does. When everything had closed down and it was late enough that there probably wouldn’t be much traffic anymore, I went back to the place and luckily the colony was still there, croaking. The next day I met a birdwatcher who told me about this Facebook group, “Thai Biodiversity Survey & Species ID”, a very active, wonderful group with a lot of professionals helping each other. From then on, I used it a lot to identify the animals and plants around me. So yeah, I learned a lot about Thailand’s highly biodiverse environment through making these recordings. The sound artist and theorist Gerald Fiebig describes your work as occupying a space between pure phonography and electroacoustic composition. How do you navigate the balance between faithfully documenting a soundscape and reshaping it into something new? Is there a point at which a field recording ceases to be documentation and becomes composition? It can also be the other way around, so that the composition is already there, recorded, and therefore gets documented. I think it always depends on how one understands it and from which angle it is observed. It can be the same as with photography or other fields of art. It is documentation. And even if it is meant to be understood as a pure composition, it is still a certain kind of documentation. But I don’t really think too much about that, to be honest. It is more of a process with a life of its own. I do not try to put that much control on it. When it feels right and attracts my energy, I go on. When there is a framework or a narrative evolving around the work, even better. On the other hand, I have plenty of recordings—for example, from Iceland last year—that I have tried to work with, but they haven’t led to any fruitful progress yet. Many passages on Noumenon blur the boundaries between natural and synthetic sound. At times it becomes difficult to distinguish an animal call from a modular synthesis process or a heavily transformed recording. What attracts you to this ambiguity, and do you see electronic manipulation as a way of extending nature’s own processes rather than imposing something artificial upon them? I think it is simply another way to play around with our possible means of (creative) expression. It always depends on how one wants to channel or expand the material and shift it into another context. I think art always has something to do with a kind of communication. And what has been chosen here is communication with a certain excerpt of the surrounding environment. Within it lies a wide aesthetic sonic palette that provides a lot of interesting material for exploration. I would say I don’t have a particular plan for those sounds. I just borrow them, shapeshift and transform them into something else, and give them back to the environment. That is the whole compositional interplay. Even so, it mostly arises from experimentation, and it isn’t as if I put a lot of focus on composition and arrangement; it’s more of an improvisational process. You cycled for 2300 km. What would you say surprised you the most that you were unable to capture or to render sonically? Suprisingly it even exceeded my expectations and I was overall happy with the results and the diversity of the recordings. But… maybe the fart of a elephant, that would have been something (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Heogen have earned that confidence across several releases, and The Precipice is the clearest proof yet that the trust between Boulton and Bax runs deep enough to produce something genuinely singular. It’s the sound of two producers who stopped negotiating with each other and started finishing each other’s sentences. Designed from the ground up as a continuous listening experience The Precipice by Heogen   Touched Music has been releasing electronic music with genuine emotional depth and creative integrity since Martin Boulton founded it in the early 2000s, raising funds for Macmillan Cancer Support across its entire catalog run. Heogen, the collaborative project of Boulton under his Min-Y-Llan alias and Dutch producer Jeroen Bax (exm), has been one of the label’s most consistent and distinctive voices, fusing Bax‘s technically complex compositional instincts with Boulton‘s melodic and rhythmical sensibility across a catalog that includes Odd Radio Circle, Inantiphsea, and the project’s self-titled release. The Precipice marks a clear shift in how the duo present their work, stripped of individual track titles, structured as numbered phases, and designed from the ground up as a continuous listening experience rather than a collection of separate pieces.​ Eight tracks labeled Phase 1 through Phase 7, followed by “Untitled Phase,” the only departure from the naming structure, and a deliberate one. The Precipice plays like an extended live set rather than an album in the conventional sense, each phase bleeding into the next, building across melodies and drums without signposting the transitions. The structure carries a clear argument: a single sustained musical idea, developed with patience and deep investment, contains more possibility than most artists allow themselves to explore. Repetition and variation aren’t opposing forces on this record. They work as partners, each pass through the central melodic territory revealing something that wasn’t visible the pass before. A genuine achievement :: The album shows the full strength of Heogen‘s melodic side alongside their downtempo electronic architecture. The production throughout is outstanding in its melodic composure, held consistently across the full runtime without losing focus or momentum. That kind of sustained quality across eight phases running to nearly an hour is a genuine achievement and speaks directly to how well Boulton and Bax understand each other’s instincts at this point in their collaboration. “Phase 6” is the highlight. The drums here are the hardest on the release, a unique chord progression running alongside choir samples that play right in the pocket with the rhythm before the track builds further outward. It’s the moment on the album where the melodic and rhythmic sides of Heogen‘s identity hit simultaneously and at full force. “Untitled Phase” closes the album as a sober and considered final statement after an intense extended session of melodies and beats. A magical arp fades in and out while chords play and sub bass runs through the low end. Within that framework there’s a subtle peace—a piano excerpt appearing quietly, followed by the sound of slow breathing in the background that makes the track stranger and more affecting the longer you sit with it. The breathing doesn’t announce itself. It’s barely audible, placed underneath everything else, and its presence humanizes the entire close of the record. Heogen have earned that confidence across several releases, and The Precipice is the clearest proof yet that the trust between Boulton and Bax runs deep enough to produce something genuinely singular. It’s the sound of two producers who stopped negotiating with each other and started finishing each other’s sentences. The Precipice is available on Touched Music. [Bandcamp] The Precipice by HeogenThe post Heogen :: The Precipice (Touched Music) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A project that Al Kooper supported and saw to publication after he left Blood Sweat & Tears: songs that "fell out of the head of" 19-year old guitarist and singer-songwriter, John Parker Compton and his three Boston-based collaborators/friends. It was the first time in a New York City recording studio (Columbia) for all four of the young musicians. One amplifier. One violin and one cello with no overdubs. No original percussion instrument, just a 17-year old bass player. 1. "Tulu Rogers" (3:57) a folk song that feels quite like an early DONOVAN song when it's just John Parker and his guitar. Once his strings companions join in there is the feeling as if an entire section of orchestra strings has joined in--and yet there is also a strong charge of Rock 'n' Roll energy being channeled by the simple music as well. This is a song that I feel could/would've been quite popular with the lyrics-driven public. (9/10)2. "Thoughts For Polly" (5:48) gentle acoustic guitar folk music which is enhanced from the start by alto saxophone, electrified harpsichord, and Country-Western drumming. A very powerful, haunting, and poetic song that is greatly augmented by the contributions of the strings and "weird" (the recorded tape being played backwards) saxophone notes. Though this is by far the album's longest song, it exudes such a comforting vibe that it feels just right--a welcome balm from start to finish. A top three song for me. (9.125/10)3. "Feathers" (2:27) two arpeggiated guitar chords set the stage for the joinder of John Parker's chamber strings companions (as well as Al Kooper's guitar and Artie Schreck's sensitive drums). The vocal performance, style, and lyrics give the song a feel of something between the gentle side of Mick Jagger (think "As Tears Go By") and Jim Croce. (9/10)4. "Bi-Weekly" (3:33) opening with a little of the Baroque pep of a Burt Bacharach or Jimmy Webb tune, oboe, organ, drums, and full orchestra support continue to launch this wonderful vocal into the realm of those two master composers. Awesome chord shift into the wonderful chorus. Another top three song. (9.125/10)5. "Glossolalia" (4:06) open sea sounds like seagulls and waves open this one before John Parker and his string quartet join in with Bobby Colomby's percussion, Al Kooper's Vibraphone play, and Tony Ackerman's additional guitar to create the gentle folk music to back John Parker's near-talking Van Morrison-like vocal performance. I don't particularly like this vocal styling but I love the mood set up by the beautiful music. (9/10) 6. "Rivers Run To The Sea" (3:30) uptempo folk-rock music that sets up a Gordon Lightfoot/Jim Croce/AL STEWART-like vocal performance. After 90 seconds in one motif, the music slows down and becomes much more intentional for its chorus, but then the horse hooves and violin pick back up to return to the verse motif. So like Al Stewart! An awesome composition rendered beautifully. (9.125/10)7. "Pascal's Paradox" (3:21) a song that Al allowed to remain untouched the way John Parker and his quartet had originally arranged it. Sounds a lot like Jim Croce's "I Got a Name." Were I into lyrics this song might have earned higher marks from me; as it is it's a nice little Baroque Chamber Pop Folk tune.(8.75/10)8. "Yesterday's Roads" (3:19) opening with the two strings players before guitar, bass, drums, and "toy" piano (upper register) join in with John Parker's Dylan-like vocal. The music plays out like something from a jazzier yet-melancholic realm--like something by Phoebe Snow, Gordon Lightfoot or Roddy Frame (Aztec Camera)--or, from the modern day, Alisdair MacLean (The Clientele) or the late Nick Talbot (Gravenhurst) and so many other "sensitive" singer-songwriters. (8.875/10)9. "Now That I Want You" (2:32) the most animated song on the album is ramped up to Brit Rock standards by the contribution of Charlie Calello's full orchestra. (8.667/10)10. "Georgia Street" (4:44) a song that is enhanced by guest appearances from Al on electric piano, Blood, Sweat & Tears drummer, Bobby Colomby, and, later in the song, Fred Lipsius' saxophone, this Chamber Folk song achieves the amazing feat of replicating with uncanny accuracy a Moody Blues-like Mellotron with just two strings players! Very cool final minute. (9.125/10)11. "Rosalie" (4:28) reminds me of a cross between Jim Croce, early Elton John, and The Rolling Stones. (8.875/10)Total time 41:45Al's reverence for artists like Bob Dylan, The Band, The Allman Brothers, and The Rolling Stones really shines through with the production and enhancements he added to John Parker's original tracks. B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of wonderfully-precocious Baroque Chamber Pop Folk gently and masterfully nurtured and produced by Columbia Records via up-and-coming musical catalyst Al Kooper.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The world's first and pre-eminent Jazz-Rock band releases their first album, thanks to Columbia Records, on February 28, 1968. Led by multi-instrumentalist musical genius Al Kooper and former Blues Project mate Steve Katz. The band was focused and committed to sporting a James Brown-like horn section as well as orchestral accompaniments. 1. "Overture" (1:33) talk about a Frank Zappa influence! This is classical symphonic music with a track of uncontrolled laughter (one might say, lunacy). It's taking The Beatles' George Martin effect and Frank Zappa eclectic skills and absurdism to new levels! (4.625/5)2. "I Love You More Than You'll Ever Know" (5:58) blues-based organ, bass & drums with electric rock guitar and very skilled lead vocals. What a great James Brown-like horn arrangement, great female background vocal "ooo's," great guitar sounds (both lead and rhythm) as well as a very zoned-in lead vocal of some powerful lyrics from Al Kooper. The finale is incredible! I wish it weren't faded out. Wow! This kind of perfection I was not expecting (from a debut album launched in 1968). (10/10)3. "Morning Glory" (4:15) a solid, polished, professional song that does little to (9/10)4. "My Days Are Numbered" (3:18) a song whose Soul gravity predicts the band's monster hits of the near future as well as sounding exactly like Paul Weller's transitional music from The Jam to The Style Council, it's is blessed with an amazingly intricate overal construct of multiple motifs all arranged and performed with such feeling, plus possessing an amazingly-catchy chorus. (9.75/10)5. "Without Her" (2:41) the jazzy/lounge side of the band with a poppy Brit-Pop swing to it and more distinctly-defined individual instrumental sounds and performances (piano, bass, jazz drums, trumpet, sax, close intimate vocal performance) as well as Jobim-like Spanish guitar play serving as the rhythm guitar. Awesome both musically and as an brainworm. (10/10)6. "Just One Smile" (4:37) another wonderfully-arranged and -rendered musical landscape with more of Jim Fielder's awesome electric bass play, Al's vulnerable and emotional vocal and incredible horn section . Weirdly, the chorus is the song's weakest element as it doesn't quite deliver the promise that the verses seem to build toward. I love the little Baroque interplay of the lute and keyboard in the instrumental passage in the first half of the fourth minute! (9.375/10) 7. "I Can't Quit Her" (3:39) opening with some Burt Bacharach like piano play of a few chords before the bass and drums enter, followed soon thereafter by Al's reverb-treated vocal and the accents of the Beatles-like horn section. Strings and female choir back the first chorus section before routing the band back into a repeat of the verse section. Then around 2:30 there is a powerful transition to a heavier, more emotional instrumental section which plays out to the final fade-out of the music with no other return of the vocal/lyrics. Awesome! What creative song construction! (9.25/10) 8. "Meagan's Gypsy Eyes" (3:24) starting out with gently-picked acoustic guitar the song then amps up with the arrival of horns and a weird keyboard. There are ample effects applied to the anachronistic keys and doubled-up vocal track, this song travels with a fairly thin and simple psychedelic sound palette until the chorus when the horns and strings get involved. This sounds a lot like something from DONOVAN, The 13th Floor Elevators, or even one of the British Baroque Pop making their way across The Pond. Steve Katz' lead vocal is great for the delivery of the song's folkie-psychedelic lyrics but he's nowhere near as strong or powerful as Al Kooper; he's more of a gnome-like delivery person. Still, this is a cool, interesting, and, ultimately, memorable song. (9/10)9. "Something' Going On" (8:00) pure JAMES BROWN bluesy R&B with each and every instrument being asked to play at their loudest and most concise/compact forms while Al sings a purely blues-oriented . Steve Katz' electric guitar solo in the third minute is surprisingly loud while also benefitting from enough distortion to make it sound like something between Eric Clapton and Jimi Hendrix. Even Steve's ensuing rhythm guitar play behind Al's piano solo in the fourth minute is loud: way louder than Al's piano. The horns, too, are really loud as Al returns to the vocal, singing as if he's trying to incite some loud audience participation/response. Tenor sax starts to solo beneath Al's call & response-like vocals. At the end of the seventh minute the music thins and returns to the form of the opening section for the band and Al to pull it to a close--but then they really ramp things up again for the finish! Great drumming from Bobby Colomby! (13.25/15) 10. "House In The Country" (3:04) a peppy little song that with multiple vocal tracks that sounds like something from a sophisticated British pop band (not The Stones or Who, more Beatles) and then they inject some of the the Zappa-like absurdist humor with ancillary voice-acted tracks. Interesting. (8.875/10) 11. "The Modern Adventures Of Plato, Diogenes And Freud" (4:12) delicate voice with chamber strings support again remind one of British Baroque Pop bands as Al sings over the top with a sincerity and literacy that sounds/feels like contemporary social commentary poetry being sung (but, again, previews an artist like Paul Weller). (9/10)12. "So Much Love / Underture" (4:43) a bit of a PROCOL HARUM sound and feel to this as Jim and Bobby lay down a funky David Axelrod-like rhythm track with Al's organ and Steve's twangy rhythm guitar strokes. Horns and background choir vocals join in from time to time, usually in bridges and sometimes in the verse passages and then over the choruses. For the final 90 seconds there is a simple pulsing organ note punctuated by brass chord blasts before the strings and weird organ oscillation sounds join in. Could've come from a West End musical. (8.75/10) Total time 49:24There are many times when the clever, sophisticated songs on this album remind me of the genius of artists like The Moody Blues, Pete Townsend, Paul McCartney, Brian Auger, and James Brown.A/five stars; a ground-breaking masterpiece of R&B/Rock Fusion (what we've all come to refer to as "Brass Rock"), one of the finest debut albums to ever explode onto the 1960s music scene.

items.body: Review by HogweedOfTuscany — I'm no stranger to controversy, but in a world full of internet contrarians and outright trolling, I feel obligated to particularly explain why this album - possibly the most well-known prog album, with immaculate sales and even more immaculate production and famous cover, the album that would make Pink Floyd not only a household name, but classic rock legends on its own - gets the measly three stars from me. Especially as back in secondary school, Pink Floyd used to be my favourite band, after taking the torch from Led Zeppelin - and despite "getting" Floyd as much as a fan can, I honestly had trouble with the general adoration even back then. How dare I? Well, let's see.I'll start with the obvious - there is way too little actual musical ideas on this album. Before you bring out your pitchforks, just count with me - Speak to Me is a short amusical collage, Breathe is a very nice acoustic shuffle that A. isn't really a finished song as such, B. is nonetheless repeated three times over the course of the relatively short album with variations that don't really make it deserved, On the Run is more or less a half-musical failed experiment (I realise it's supposed to support the concept - which I'll get to later - being a psychological embodiment of the hectic modern world, anxiety and paranoia, but the execution itself is severely lacking - Waters would get much better at these "psychology first" unpleasant electronic detours on the latter albums, like with Welcome to the Machine), Time is great, but VERY similar to Breathe (to the level of me not even recognising when the song shifted into the Breathe Reprise on my first listen), Great Gig in the Sky, whether you like it or not, is more or less an unstructured, gospellish vocal performance (that more or less stands or falls on the shoulders of the vocalist), Eclipse is just an outro to Brain Damage that doesn't really deserve being considered a separate song and that leaves us with four finished, complete songs on the album: Time, Money, Us and Them and Brain Damage. Of these, Money switches its great flow and rhythm into a frankly somewhat pedestrian jamming session (I mean, I have collected Floyd bootlegs and loved their solos and such, but this one doesn't feel particularly inspired), Us and Them (despite being my second favourite off the record) is way too overlong for such a slow-trodding funeral dirge on a second half of the album, Brain Damage annoys me for reasons I'll get into in the next paragraph and Time feels way too lethargic for a song that's the definite highlight of the album. But I suppose my biggest issue with the album is that it's too... approachable. It doesn't really dabble in poetry, in anything even slightly highbrow, it does away with allegory and just confronts you with the ideas and the concept, with all the power and all the grace of a small-town thinker. "Too didactic" is probably the word that came to mind most, on this most recent listen. You're being told and explained and preached to by Roger Waters (who certainly isn't the person to be doing so) what he doesn't like about the world this time and how you should approach your life accordingly. Without any subtlety or nuance, in the great tradition of Bob Dylan around cca 1964. This honestly makes all the concessions to the concept of the album even worse, because this higher purpose is eventually somewhat disappointing. "But hey, Hogweed," you say, "don't you also often complain about the times prog bands were way TOO obtuse and too much detached from reality, crawled up their own intestine, like with The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway?" Well, yes, neither extreme is preferable, honestly, but one is certainly more artful than the other. But I understand that the honestly unimaginable commercial success was also caused by this, much like by Parson's production and so on. But to me, it's way too little, delivered in a somewhat underwhelming way primarily by a person who certainly shouldn't be in the position of a guru, though his descent into the Everbile was yet to come on the following albums. And taking itself way too seriously, with an undeserved weight. But I admit that the sentence "Hanging on in quiet desperation is the English way" is great and hilarious. And that brings us to my third concern, that is, some genuinely baffling decisions, especially regarding the general atmosphere and tonal coherence. Putting the most acerbic and sarcastic song Money into the mouth of Gilmour, with his inherent vocal wistfulness and melancholy, feels really weird (through a modern lens, it kinda gives off the vibe of the "old man yelling a cloud", he's just spitting the words "New car, caviar, four star daydream // Think I'll buy me a football team" but he overdoes it with the nonchalance, sounding more confused than anything). The jams don't really leave an impression on me, they're not nostalgic, they're not mindful, they're just as lethargic as the rest of the album. Nice, but really not outstanding. And Great Gig... while realising I'm probably going to make myself some new enemies now, I don't really like the song, nor do I understand the enthrallment that it elicits in so many people. I am quite well-versed in American soul music (from Otis Redding and Sam Cooke to Aretha and Diana Ross), I understand its appeal, but A. I find the combination with Floyd's particular English jazzy melancholy really doesn't work for me, and it sticks out from the album like a sore thumb, B. honestly, I just dislike Clare Torry's vocals, the timbre, the overwrought histrionics of it all. I realise that's just me and that I might be the only person in the world to find the performance more grating than anything, but especially as an artistic representation of death and the afterlife, probably the highest concept the album ever aspires to, it's way off the mark for me, all the more since it's positioned more or less as the centrepiece of the album.Not to drown too much in a sea of negativity - don't want to end up like Waters, after all - the things that really work about this album REALLY work, and I can see very well how the DSOTM mirage can captivate the listener. All the flaws I mentioned above, despite being really hard to stomach for me, are exceptionall well hidden. You don't really notice that they've been revisiting Breathe for the third time once they start their elevator jam in Any Colour You Like - not at first, at least. The heartbeats, the spoken snippets, the general flow and the audio quality, the catchy 7/8 of Money - it does give off the vibe of the lads being so apparently pleased with themselves were more or less justified. There are famous works of art that deserve its stature way less. So ignore the lyrics and raise my rating to four stars. Or go listen to Wish You Were Here and Animals.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Vanden Plas playing progressive metal before its time. This 13th album, a cathedral of sound, picks up where the acoustic "AcCult" left off 30 years later."Far Off Grace," from the album of the same name, shines on the acoustic guitar, which understood that more than just noise was needed. Stephan excels, Alessandro captivates, Andy enchants with his uniquely melancholic voice; the Andalusian solo before the furious finale, restrained, neoclassical, progressive, hypnotic layering these musical textures. "Holes in the Sky" from "Seraphic Clockwork" follows the same pattern, a slow, melodic build-up stripped of electric guitar; a relaxing track with a 6-string acoustic solo. Andy's warm vocals make this a radical departure from the original heavy metal vibe. "The Ghost Experiment" has a Maiden United feel, with the drums letting the bass drums lay down the rhythm and power. An Andalusian, Celtic, and refined folk solo, captivating, oscillates between drama and melancholic joy. "Boat on the River," a Styx cover, accentuates the Celtic feel, the introspective guitar, the accordion a poignant memory, sailing between the Balkans, Greece, and a New Orleans port."Healing Tree" from "Beyond Daylight" features crystalline piano and a cinematic atmosphere with the flute. A vocal duet ballad by Andy and Katri from Numento, the female voice. The piano, the two-tone break, the solemn, archaic prog on Marillion, the Irish flute. Memory, relaxation, wisdom, emphasis. "Postcard to God" from "Christ 0" is a crystalline stereo-melodic vibration with shifting tempos. Andy leads this mellowed metal ship, while Stephan weaves in a folk tune before Alessandro's pre-Genesisian, saccharine solo. "Nothing Else Matters" features a stripped-down piano guiding Andy down a new dramatic path, the dark strings adding to its delicate sensitivity. A stunning Metallica cover, giving you goosebumps. "You Fly" from "The God Thing," piano and guitar, Maiden United again?go listen to them. The complex track, richer with its velvety keyboards and the surprising addition of John's sax from Supertramp. The sensual, contemplative melody, the captivating guitar-saxophone break, the almost heavy bass rhythm?a musical paradigm. The latent, progressive build-up, the sustained riff, the piano and saxophone solo?reminiscent of '80s Phil Collins and Dire Straits. A fresh, jazzy, marshmallowy feel that culminates in a wild, heavy finale. (3.75)

items.body: Review by kev rowland — If one goes back in time to the very early days of Martin Springett the musician, he was in a band called Gateway Driver in 1973 and played in Germany with bassist Rob Burns. Rob later worked with the likes of David Gilmour, Pete Townshend, and Eric Burdon, was professor at Otago University as well as being an author of different books on music. When Martin released the wonderful 'The Gardening Club' album in 1983, the keyboard player John Sheard, who has since appeared on hundreds of recordings with artists such as, Rita Mcneil, Olivia Newton-John, Ian and Sylvia, Dan Hill, Rita Coolidge, Mary Margaert O'Hara, Celine Dion, and many more. This song came about after Martin survived a major heart operation, and now he is again fighting various issues he decided to finally complete the song, as he always liked it but never felt there was room for it on 'The Riddle'. In many ways he has used musicians who document the journey he has been through, as alongside Rob and John we also have Kevin Laliberte who has worked closely with Martin for the last five years. The quartet may never have been in the same room together (Rob still lives in NZ and the rest of the guys are in Canada), but it never feels that way, as here they sound as if the band are playing and smiling at each other as they work through a song which never feels as if it is more than eight minutes long. It is undoubtedly one of Martin's finest pieces to date, wonderfully layered with the warmth of Camel combining with some of the detachment of Pink Floyd, all brought together with stacks of Roy Harper to make something which is truly special. I found the best way to truly appreciate this song is to put it on repeat and just let it play for a few hours as each time there is something else which comes to light, making this majestic and wonderful. Is it the multi-tracked and slightly distorted slide guitars here, or the layered keyboards there, the feeling that Martin's acoustic guitar and vocals are always at the heart of everything, with bass which is warm and reflective, driving when needed to?I have no idea, but yet again I can only wonder what would have happened if 'The Gardening Club' had received the credit it so richly deserved more than 40 years ago. Would Martin now be a household name in the music industry? Given the quality (and remarkable quantity) of his output since 2018 I can only imagine. I know I feel warmed by his friendship and feel real joy and empathy when listening to songs such as this. This is currently only available as a digital single on Bandcamp, and for just $2 what have you got to lose? If you know his music then you will delight in this, and if you have yet to come across Martin then this is the perfect introduction.

items.album: Read an extract from  Aftershock: The Seismic Impact Of Dubstep
items.excerpt: In this extract, taken from the chapter “Mystical Warriors”, Laurie Osborne aka Appleblim and Sam Shackleton recall the development of their influential Skull Disco label Appleblim: Shackleton’s a unique character. items.body: In this extract, taken from the chapter “Mystical Warriors”, Laurie Osborne aka Appleblim and Sam Shackleton recall the development of their influential Skull Disco label Appleblim: Shackleton’s a unique character. He’s extremely well read and speaks at least five languages – but he’s also hilarious, one of the funniest people I’ve ever met. When you get someone’s humour and realise that they’re also a deep thinker? That’s heaven to me. We lived in Stoke Newington in the period that we were going to FWD>> together. Shackleton: I ended up in London by accident, you see. I was living in Turkey, married to a Hungarian woman, and when that relationship ended, I moved to Leiden, in the Netherlands, with the idea of making quick money in a tulip-packing factory. But when I got there, there was no work for me, so I called a friend in London and told him I had nowhere to stay. I moved over right away, some time between 1999 or 2000, and that turned into a decade in London. Appleblim: Shackleton was playing at squat parties under the incredible name of Bleach Bastard, in a group called Evil Mastermind with an MC, Vengeance Tenfold. Shackleton: Vengeance Tenfold was a squatter, so he always knew a place where we could perform. We wanted to be, in essence, a krautrock band with drum machines. We were listening to dancehall, punk and drum ’n’ bass, and that want for bass and beat science led to a want for big sound systems, rather than just what was in use at the squat parties. Appleblim: Shackleton had already been making weird bass music, with a dancehall vibe, and when he went to FWD>>, he basically went, “Oh, I can take what I’ve already been making, up the tempo and have it fit in with all of this”. It was his desire to put out a release in that vein that turned us into Skull Disco. He’s from Lancashire and I’m sort of from the Midlands – I was born in Derby, and my Mum’s from the North – so we share a love of that self-deprecating Northern humour. Skull Disco is “school disco” in a Northern accent. We were huge fans of comedians like Chris Morris, Sacha Baron Cohen and Tim Vine, but what really bonded us was a love for heavy, weird bands, like Throbbing Gristle, Crass and The Fall. We read William Burroughs and punk rock fanzines – Shackleton ran a fanzine up North, too – and connected over percussive trance, hardcore dub reggae, ragga and noise music. Shackleton: When I was 15 or 16 years old, I was putting on bands in my hometown, which is Nelson in Lancashire. I was very DIY. When you come from a small town, especially back then, you had to make your own entertainment, so I got into punk rock. I did run a fanzine – that and the local gigs fed into each other. I’d write about experimental rock bands like Jesus Lizard, Suicide, Nomeansno and Throbbing Gristle. Appleblim: That’s what we, as Skull Disco, had that the London lot didn’t have. Their sound was distilled out of garage and drum ’n’ bass, and Shackleton liked industrial, Muslimgauze and sacred Indian music. He wasn’t a raver. He didn’t come from techno and he didn’t understand the appeal of house or garage music – but he was into music from around the world that induces a trance state when you’re dancing to it, which is what we got at FWD>>. We’d get home from FWD>>, get on the decks and play King Tubby, Prince Far I and Dillinja, to keep that physical force rolling. The Plastic People sound system was so powerful, so clean, so precise, that when you did start getting this combination of bass and percussion, it was an out of body experience. Shackleton: Even though Laurie and I weren’t squatters, that’s where the Skull Disco party roots are, and it was quite a different crowd than the London club scene. The enjoyable thing was just being together; having wild times, if you will. We were always up for the parties – you can read into that what you want – but we were also looking for something different musically. I’m not really interested in melodies, but I also didn’t want to make tracks that are purely for chin-strokers. I was never interested in four-to-the-floor music. It never did it for me on any level. I was always into dub: proper, heaving, big bass; that body music. I wanted beats that were interesting, demanding; not obviously in any formula. It would be wrong to say that the DJs and producers at FWD>> were tapping into the spirit of, say, Throbbing Gristle, but I saw the party as avant garde in its own way. All of the elements I liked existed in one place. Then, instead of working at any bpm – which I do, and have done since – I brought my beats into that FWD>> range of 135-140 bpm. Your body does absorb that bpm as a prototype, unconsciously, when you’re on a dancefloor like that. Appleblim: We’re not Jamaican, we’re not Rastafarians, but having listened to so much dub, so many soundclashes, that got infused into Skull Disco. We riffed off the idea of the Soundboy being twisted in different ways: Soundboy gets buried, murdered, turned to ash, chopped up and snorted; we commit this Soundboy to the ground! We loved the epicness of reggae with its Biblical references, of Holy Mount Zion and Daniel in the Lion’s Den, and used it as a contrast with our dark Northern humour. Shackleton: There’s nothing worthwhile in life that doesn’t have humour with it, and the sooner you come to that realisation the sooner you win. That’s probably the only bit of wisdom I have. Even Prince Far I himself, the don of dread, could be funny as hell. Appleblim: Exactly. Within reggae, there’s so much humour: in the Yard tapes, where they’re calling out what food they like, calling out to each other, telling silly stories amongst that spiritual dread; stuff like the Kingston story of “The baker uses poison flour!” We didn’t know exactly what it meant when we heard those songs, but what we did hear were these larger than life characters – and that’s what we wanted to tap into with Skull Disco. Aftershock: The Seismic Impact Of Dubstep is published by Velocity Press. Read Derek Walmsley's review of the book in The Wire 511. Subscribers can also read the review online in the digital library.

items.body: To someone who still buys physical CDs, following the partnership of Gustavo Dudamel and the Los Angeles Philharmonic over the past several years has proven frustrating, since most of their albums are available via download or streaming only. I enjoyed their 2021 Ives symphony cycle, the Dvořák Symphonies Nos. 7-9 (2022), and their thrilling account of Prokofiev’s complete Romeo and Juliet, released earlier this year. (All of these are on DG, though only the Ives is available as a physical product.) Now Dudamel and the orchestra present Schumann’s four symphonies, recorded live in 2018 and released by Platoon. Schumann Symphonies Amazon Apple In excellent liner notes, Andrew Mellor writes that Schumann’s first symphony “reaches heights of joyousness that he would never quite attain again.” That joy is the chief characteristic of Dudamel’s reading. It is played with infectious energy, tempos lean toward the faster end of the spectrum, and the orchestra’s unanimity of attack and articulation is a constant delight. The strings have a luscious sheen, with distinctive woodwinds and bright, resonant brass. The Cleveland recordings of Szell and Dohnányi (Sony and Decca) may offer an even greater level of technical finesse, but neither reaches the “heights of joyousness” heard in Los Angeles. In the second symphony, Dudamel seems hesitant to engage with the work’s darker emotional terrain. This is not a programmatic work, but I believe it captures a progression from debilitating depression to joyful health. (Schumann wrote: “I wrote the symphony…when I was unwell… I began to feel more myself when I wrote the last movement, but it was only after I had completed the whole score that I felt any better.”) In the first movement’s development, the disintegration of melodic material and harmonic instability express those struggles, as does the obsessively repeating figure driving the music toward the end of the movement. With Dudamel those moments are too easy, lacking the intensity heard in readings by Bernstein (Vienna Philharmonic/DG) and Luisi (Vienna Symphony/Orfeo). After a brilliantly played Scherzo (with a thrilling Coda), the deeply felt, sweetly sung slow movement minimizes the agony heard in those Viennese recordings. The triumphant final movement is excitingly played but has less emotional power because the victory was too easily reached. The Rhenish is more successful: the horns bray thrillingly in the opening movement, and the Scherzo is lithe and playful. I found the third movement less convincing, lacking the delicate balletic quality of the best performances; perhaps the engineered sound has an ambience that casts a gauze over the softer playing. But the fourth movement brings a potent sense of brooding and wonder, followed by a high-spirited finale in which the horns again excel, finishing with an exultant Coda. Gustavo Dudamel. The reading of the fourth symphony is in some ways the most interesting, because Dudamel makes original interpretive choices. The opening movement is slower than Szell, Dohnányi, Karajan (Vienna/DG), and Luisi, and Dudamel chooses to relax into that tempo instead of creating a sense of forward propulsion. This generates a gentler, more settled mood than any other performance I know. The Romanze is forlorn and achingly tender, followed by a lithe and elegant Scherzo, though I feel Dudamel’s Trios veer into sentimentality. The final movement again downplays the darker moments — I am used to something stormier (like Karajan’s final 1987 account with the Vienna Philharmonic). I am not entirely convinced that this reading is what Schumann intended, but it intrigued me each time I listened and made me think about this symphony in a different way. The liner notes (not readily available on all platforms) include biographical sketches of the orchestra and conductor, a full orchestral roster, and Mellor’s erudite essay. As noted above, the recordings were made eight years ago; why did it take so long to release them? Perhaps a decision was made to release them now to honor the seventeen-year partnership between this orchestra and its outgoing Music Director. That is something worthy of celebration, and I hope that Dudamel’s tenure with the New York Philharmonic will be just as fruitful. Recommended Comparisons Schumann: Complete Symphonies George Szell | Christoph von Dohnányi | Leonard Bernstein | Fabio Luisi The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: In his booklet interview with Michelle Assay for Lunaris, Bruce Liu discusses his fascination with the night and his inner world of sound. The program includes familiar works like Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata alongside pieces by Mompou, Cage, and Agnes Obel. Lunaris Amazon Presto Apple Liu notes that Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata anchors the curation. A major point of interest is Beethoven’s marking that the entire first movement be played without dampers (senza sordini). On a modern piano, this implies holding the damper pedal down continuously, an approach that can be problematic given the instrument’s resonance compared to a fortepiano. Liu’s pedaling remains clean throughout. While the Adagio sostenuto (track 2) leans toward the austere, it communicates the intended solemnity. The Allegretto is deliberate without becoming mannered in its elegance, while the Presto agitato (track 4) introduces the necessary intensity. Liu’s precise fingerwork prevents the textures from becoming oversaturated, and the subito accents drive the volatility and urgency central to the movement. Beethoven’s Sonata Op. 53 (Waldstein) serves as a thoughtful pairing with the Moonlight. The opening movement (track 8) captures the con brio spirit with tight articulation and clarity, and Liu’s decision to highlight select secondary voices adds dimension to the reading. The Introduzione (track 9) is calm, yet Liu uses moments of inflection toward its close to generate the suspense needed to connect to the final movement. The finale reflects the sonata’s L’Aurore nickname: Liu’s pedaling imparts the haze of dawn upon the opening theme (where Beethoven again asks for the pedal to be held). As the music reaches its climax, the textures become drier, resulting in an unusually crisp presentation. Scriabin’s Sonata No. 4 in F-sharp major (tracks 16-17) presents two distinct shades of anticipation. In the Andante, Liu demonstrates sensitivity and imagination, projecting a different tonal shade for each shifting harmony. This quiet yearning builds tension that is released in the Prestissimo volando. He navigates the rapid passages with precision and a certain lightness, the larger sections stay controlled without feeling subdued, and the movement’s trajectory of intensity is clearly shaped. While Debussy’s Clair de lune might seem an expected inclusion given the program’s theme, Liu opts instead for the composer’s Rêverie (track 5). From the hypnotic ostinato that opens the work, he builds a multicolored reading that alternates between lush and enigmatic textures. Across this range of expression, Liu’s bell-like tone maintains structural cohesion. Bruce Liu. Photo © Bartek Barczyk. Agnes Obel’s Tokka (track 7) is a meaningful addition in both genre and artistry. Through the music’s relative sparseness and concise phrases, Liu conveys transience and fragility. Similarly concise in phrasing, the first of Arnold Schoenberg’s 6 Kleine Klavierstücke, Op. 19 (track 14) offers an alternative perspective: Liu highlights the work’s angularity through a hushed tone, sharp articulation, and a persistent sense of enigma. Note that the Schoenberg, along with Reynaldo Hahn’s Hivernale, appears only on the digital and vinyl editions of the album; the CD omits both tracks. Liu takes a notable approach to the final work, John Cage’s Dream. Across the thrice-repeated material, he uses three different keyboards between two pianos (noting in the booklet that one instrument features two keyboards), and the effect is perceptible: each iteration has a distinct character, with the second sounding appropriately distant and murky. Throughout, Liu’s playing combines reflection, declamation, and meditation, emphasizing the structure of Cage’s minimalism. In a concept album of this nature, hearing directly from the artist is valuable. The detailed interview with Assay serves as an important companion to the program, presenting Liu as an introspective and articulate musician. His commentary aligns with performances that are insightful and reward a dedicated listen. items.body: ÆRIA released “Ivy” on August 4, 2026, the second of six tracks on the self-released EP “Ivy: The First Mini-Album”. The project mixes operatic vocals with synthpop basslines and coldwave textures, and describes itself on its own YouTube channel as “an operatic darkwave girl group from a fantasy music universe”. No label is credited: the copyright and phonogram lines on the release both read ÆRIA. What is on ÆRIA’s ‘Ivy: The First Mini-Album’ The EP runs 19 minutes and 26 seconds across six tracks: “Stargirls (Intro)” (1:30), “Ivy” (3:25), “Bright Side Of The Moon” (4:04), “In Her Hands” (4:46), “Ivy (Reprise)” (3:12) and “Stargirls (Outro)” (2:27). The two “Stargirls” pieces bracket the record and “Ivy” returns in a reprise, so the running order is built as a single arc rather than a set of separate songs. The release is on Spotify; no physical edition and no Bandcamp page have been confirmed. The band’s own promotional material presents “Ivy” as a debut single. On the release itself it appears as an album track, and the EP carries a single date of August 4, 2026 for all six pieces. The accompanying “ÆRIA – IVY (Official Music Video)” runs 3:27 and was posted to the group’s YouTube channel, which also carries a short clip titled “How ÆRIA Began”. About ÆRIA ÆRIA is a new project with a short public record, so much of its history is not yet documented. What is confirmed comes from the group’s own channels and from the release itself. The project presents itself as a fantasy girl group whose music, artwork and narrative are built as one continuous story, and it states openly that it is AI-rendered, describing the technology as an artistic canvas rather than something to conceal. Correspondence sent to press on behalf of the project is signed by a member using the name Cerulean Blue. The group maintains a YouTube channel at @weareaeria, an Instagram account at @weareaeria and a TikTok account at @aeriaband. Its first release, “Ivy: The First Mini-Album”, arrived on August 4, 2026 without a label, distributor or producer credit attached to it. Side-Line previously covered a comparable case in The mysterious case of Ella Rey – An AI darkwave artist, where an AI-generated darkwave project built a substantial streaming audience without disclosing how the recordings were made; ÆRIA differs in stating the method up front. No live dates, further releases or member names have been announced.
