items.body: As a young shoegaze kid flirting with goth at the turn of the century, discovering Projekt Records was an absolute game changer for me. For several years, I worshipped the label and its prolific roster, soaking up each new release by Mira, Audra, Mors Syphilitica, Love Spirals Downwards, Lovesliescrushing, vidnaObmana, Unto Ashes, and many more. My obsession with the label culminated in a pilgrimage with three online friends to Philadelphia in 2002, where I spent a long summer weekend at the Trocadero for ProjektFest, the label’s regular showcase. Good times, noodle salad. For the uninitiated, Projekt began in 1983 as a DIY outlet for ambient/synth artist Sam Rosenthal. A few years later, Rosenthal began collaborating with like-minded musicians under the name Black Tape for a Blue Girl. As the flagship artist on Projekt, Blacktape began to thrive by the mid-1990s, by which point their introspective, Brian Eno-meets-Dead Can Dance sound attracted a devout cult following. Over the course of forty years, Black Tape for a Blue Girl have released thirteen studio records, a handful of EPs, and several compilation-only tracks. Their work continues to innovate and inspire. This October, Rosenthal will be releasing a 40th anniversary expanded reissue of Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s debut LP The Rope across a variety of formats. Released in 1986, The Rope is a strong statement of intent that continues to capture the imagination of listeners around the world. To celebrate the reissue as well as four decades of Black Tape for a Blue Girl and Projekt Records, I had the chance to catch up with Rosenthal to discuss the band’s past, present, and future, the label, and all things in between. First there was God, then there was man, then there was Black Tape for a Blue Girl… Let’s talk about the genesis of the band. You were recording ambient/minimal electronic music early on under various names and I’m curious to hear how Blacktape evolved from that work. I was making a fanzine in Florida when I was in community college in the early ‘80s. I was writing about the local bands, punk bands, new romantic bands, and whatever else was happening. I went to Radio Shack and got a Moog keyboard and started making my own somewhat formless electronic music. It was the early ’80s, there was no way people could hear most of these bands I was writing about since a lot of them were bedroom projects and not the punk/rock live show side of things, so I formed Projekt in 1983 as an outlet to release a cassette of bands from southern Florida which also featured some of my ambient work. Then I met Oscar Herrera through his band, The Sleep of Reason, who were compared to Bauhaus. When I heard his voice, I thought he was a great vocalist with a lot of range. I asked if he wanted to sing on a couple of tracks on my Islands cassette (which was reissued last year on vinyl). I went to California for college in February of ’86. I was alone and didn’t know anybody and I started writing my own lyrics. Looking back now, they were very morose and extremely introspective. For perspective, I was listening to a lot of This Mortal Coil and Dead Can Dance and Marc Almond. Those are the three bands you could mash together and consider an early reference point for Blacktape. There was also the instrumental material, Brian Eno side… I went back to Florida during summer break and asked Oscar to sing on six tracks that would feature on the first Black Tape for a Blue Girl album, The Rope. The Sleep of Reason (remastered) by The Sleep of Reason It seems like your solo work bled right into The Rope, it seemed like a natural progression in my opinion. With that in mind, I’m curious about why you decided to form the band versus continuing under either your own name or the Projekt Electronic Amerika moniker—was it about creating two separate entities as the music took on a new identity? Yeah, I think because it had vocals and the intention was to bring in more people in the band, it made sense to create a band name. Did it make sense to me? It did at the time. As you say, it really is an evolution and progression from Islands, but it was different enough to me because I was writing lyrics now, it seemed more like a band. But then again, it wasn’t, you know, the Alan Parsons Project, it wasn’t about me as the front person, I wasn’t going to be the singer. It seemed like it would be odd to release it under my name, but have Oscar be the singer. With Brian Eno, he sang, so he could have a hundred musicians and collaborators and styles, but he’s still the singer… So let’s talk about recording The Rope. Can you tell us about some of your processes and techniques along the way? So, there was a format Cassette Porta Studio which was an average cassette tape that ran at double speed and used both sides of the tape using all four tracks at once. I recorded in my dorm room with some cheap microphone I had. I had one keyboard with me at college—it was all very primitive. Then I went back to Florida to record vocals with Oscar; we recorded in his living room and did the whole album in two hours in one afternoon. He was already prepared since I sent cassettes of a rough mix of the material with me poorly singing so he could get an idea of what I was thinking as far as song and vocal structure. Since you were exclusively releasing cassettes at the time, what made you decide to release on vinyl? It was 1986, so I doubt CDs were widely available at the time… CDs existed, but I certainly didn’t have the money to make them. There was one LP before that, Tanzmusic. For The Rope, I decided to press something like 300 or 500 copies on vinyl, and that was the only way the album existed until I reissued it in 1990 on CD and cassette. How did you distribute the album at the time? Did you shop for other labels before deciding to develop Projekt into a full-fledged DIY label? Well, I had already been doing my cassettes by mail order, which we sent for a review in a magazine and some little ad somewhere and then people would write about them. I don’t remember if The Rope actually got any distribution to be honest. I remember submitting it, and I remember getting rejected by some distributors… Did they at least listen to it? I swear to God nobody listens to anything anymore… Well, that’s right, now they don’t listen. They just go, “is this in a genre we could sell?” Which might arguably be better for the band in a way, you don’t have that first filter. So yeah, I can’t say for sure if the album had much real distribution. If you have the original LP there’s a logo on the back for some company who claimed they were going to help distribution, but then they vanished. They ghosted. They thought they could market us like The Moody Blues. I was like “Uh, no, no you can’t do that…” Hey, I love The Moody Blues! I’d rather listen to them than a lot of new darkwave, no shame! Though at the time, I could imagine that’s not what you wanted to hear… No, it wasn’t, they might as well have said The Doors, you know? It felt so irrelevant to what was going on at the time and what I was trying to do. Not to die on this hill or anything, but I can see a certain classical/neoclassical thread running through some Blacktape and Moody Blues material. Maybe it’s just me since I love both bands. It’s also very minor, but I sometimes hear the more prog-like folk bands like Strawbs or Pentangle in some of your song structures, but that could just be my brain wanting to find a connection between all these adjacent genres… I mean, there were certainly some English folk and prog bands that I liked, and I loved Hero & Heroine by the Strawbs and some of Ghosts, and Dave Cousins’ Two Weeks Last Summer, but I don’t think I was really going for that, at least not intentionally. Unto Ashes certainly fit more into that category. Though I guess prog could also capture things like Tangerine Dream and some more new age and ambient material, which I do hear at the heart of much of the early Blacktape material. At the time though, it did seem like in a world of goth rock bands, there wasn’t much out there that sounded like Black Tape for a Blue Girl, so I could see how it would be hard for a distributor or reviewer to figure out what to make of you. I think if you were aware of 4AD and This Mortal Coil, you could make that connection, but yeah, a lot of reviewers said we sounded like Sisters of Mercy… No, that’s not even CLOSE! Not at all, though I guess you could argue that Oscar sounds like some of the English goth vocalists, but that’s the beginning and end of the comparison. Sisters of Mercy are a rock band. “Memory, Uncaring Friend,” the first track on The Rope is a rock song I guess, but the rest of the record isn’t rock at all! I love that song by the way. It’s one of my early favorites. It’s certainly got guitars, but it has such an unconventional beat and song structure. The guitars are almost thin and textural compared to the synths, while the beat is so prominent and treated… By “treated” you mean the echo effect because it was recorded in a garage (laughs)! We certainly weren’t able to run everything through an ARP synthesizer like Low, but we tried to capture some sort of DIY version of that. To be honest, looking back at things, I suppose The Rope would have been considered more of a demo. If I didn’t release it on Projekt I imagine a label would have wanted to re-record it after signing us, putting more money or a big producer behind it. The Rope (40th) by Black Tape For A Blue Girl But I like that about the early material, how primitive and DIY it sounds, it’s certainly part of the charm, in my opinion! So, I know you followed up The Rope really quickly… In fact, all the early Blacktape albums were recorded and released in pretty quick succession. Did you have time to refine your process? For Mesmerized by the Sirens, my school had an eight track recorder, so I expanded and started recording eight tracks instead of four. It bumped up the ability to not have to smash everything and not pingponging throughout the mix, so I could make things a little more complex. Also, there are some other textures that came into play from other musicians being involved. Walter Holland playing guitar, Sue Kenny Smith, who is the female vocalist on that record… These things added another layer to the recordings that helped us evolve. You’re right though, The Rope was 1986, Mesmerized was 1987, Ashes in the Brittle Air was 1989, and A Chaos of Desire was 1991, though I recorded it in 1990. Still a prolific run! It sounds like you did learn quite a bit over a short period of time, picking up collaborators and band members along the way… I think those first four records are really a set, a complete idea, and showcases a bit of my learning process there, too. I think A Chaos of Desire, the fourth record, is the most coherent mood of these albums, while Ashes in the Brittle Air has diverse styles. I remember bringing Ashes to a store for consignment, they listened and they asked if it was a various artists album (laughs)! Chaos brought in Vicki Richards on violin. I think the musicianship really stepped up with her on the record. She’s just so good… Where did you meet all these wild and wonderful collaborators? Well, as I mentioned, I met Oscar in Florida because of his band. Vicki I got in touch with through Slap, a project in Miami that she played with. I had written about Slap and Stephen Nester in my zine a few times and I asked him to put me in touch with her. She had several albums in the new age and world music field but she was also working with jazz musicians, so I knew she had a diverse playing style. It was a completely different thing for her to record this material, to play so passionately, which fit really well over the ambient stuff. There’s also a violinist named J’Anna Jacoby who was playing in The Black Watch at the time… Oh, I remember them! Quite jangly, if I recall… Yeah! J’Anna also plays on A Chaos of Desire, on some of the more song-like tracks. She’s now playing with Rod Stewart, in his live band! Wow, really?! The rise of Black Tape for a Blue Girl also intersects with the rise of the Projekt label. What was the first thing you put out on the label that wasn’t your own material? The first artist thing that wasn’t a solo record or a Blacktape album was a compilation of Attrition in 1990, which is pretty fitting as I still work quite closely with Martin Bowes, who does the mastering for my music. Projekt also licensed the Peyote record by O Yuki Conjugate pretty early on. That’s a really special record… Definitely. Otherwise, I think the first band that debuted on the label was Lycia. Then came Love Spirals Downward, Lovesliescrushing, and Soul Whirling Somewhere, all in quick succession. Three of the first four bands were in Arizona at the time. Projekt was originally thought of as “a southwestern label,” which is interesting since I don’t think there were that many goth bands from that area. It’s strange to me that Phoenix was such a hotspot for goth and ethereal music… There’s a whole genre I like to call “desert goth” which incorporates a lot of the early Projekt bands, things like Abecedarians and Psi Com, Red Temple Spirits, etc. alongside bands from Independent Project Records like Savage Republic and Autumnfair. There was a certain psychedelia and bleakness that ran through the scene that certainly seems to be a California/Arizona construct, which is interesting since it’s such a sunny place! Anyway, how did the first Projekt bands find you? Did you put out a call for bands? Not quite, they were all bands that sent us demos and hadn’t released anything on other labels, so I worked with the bands to develop material into their first album. Lycia and Soul Whirling Somewhere mixed their records at my place in California. I still get demos by email, so it’s a similar idea, but back then a band had to take time to make a tape and mail the tape, they had to put effort into it! So, was it always your intention to release other artists, or did it just develop naturally? I think that once Blacktape started getting some distribution and reviews, it seemed like the infrastructure existed for it. I’d been friends with Martin from Attrition since the very early 1980s when I reviewed some of his music. I figured I’d put something else out into that channel and see what happened. CDs were so expensive to make back then. The Attrition release eventually paid itself back, I decided to keep putting more things into that channel to see what would happen. The problem with early distribution though was that they weren’t really paying us. In the early 1990s, we had something going with Tower Records where we were owed $30,000, they said they’d pay SOME of that if we sent them Projekt’s new releases—blackmail basically. It was a shady business, I knew they were always going to be shitty, but they knew that I really needed the distribution. Wow. I mean I guess music industry bullshit like that has never changed, though it seems like they were a little more upfront about it back then! We can jump forward to 1997 when Projekt hooked up with Ryko for distribution and they were really professional, not a bunch of scammers ripping off bands left and right. Between having a better distribution company and getting to the age of computers, it was much easier for Projekt as a business. It wasn’t until 1991 that I could actually do Projekt full-time and in those early days we did everything by fax machine and telephone, and I was only able to focus on things here and there as I was also working on computer graphics at the time. I had two lives in those early years. I know I’m jumping around a bit, when I moved to Chicago in 1996, Projekt grew to thirteen employees. The label was pretty large and was costly, but the Blacktape albums like This Lush Garden Within and Remnants of a Deeper Purity were doing well enough to justify it. Remnants is still the best seller from the band… Well, with good reason, it seems to be the most accessible in some ways. My mom liked that album! Yeah, and it’s interesting because stylistically, it’s not really a goth album… This lush garden within by Black Tape For A Blue Girl That might be the secret though, I see it more as a classical record, which is obviously a beloved genre. I’d argue that This Lush Garden Within is the darkest record you’ve done. It’s possibly my favorite, but it’s also not an easy one to jump into as a first timer. But to follow it up with something so… beautiful, was an interesting move. 1997 and 1998 were probably the peak of the music industry, as far as selling records. I’m going to guess over time that the Remnants album sold like 17,000 copies and has been the best seller on the label for some time. But yeah, it’s not really a “goth record” to me. Though I guess if you consider Dead Can Dance goth, then maybe? Well, if you want to split hairs, I’d say the first two Dead Can Dance albums and the first EP are “goth” for sure, but they moved away from it pretty quickly. Anyway, why do you think Remnants is the best seller? Right place, right time? Absolutely. I think having Ryko distribution meant Projekt could get the album into Borders and places like that. You can’t really say that anymore… I guess not. I do see vinyl at Barnes & Noble these days, but it’s usually legacy releases and modern rock/pop artists and every Pearl Jam album in triplicate. Nothing quite as subversive as a Black Tape for a Blue Girl album… Though maybe I haven’t been looking hard enough. Well, our reissues are available to Barnes & Noble at this point, but it’s just a matter of someone from a particular location ordering one! At the same time, Projekt was putting out Lycia’s Cold and Excelsis: A Dark Noel, both of which did really well, and I think I have the Ryko distribution to thank for that. If Remnants of Deeper Purity had come out three years earlier, would it have been the right time for it? You know, hard to say! On a related note, what Blacktape album would you suggest for a first-time listener? Man, I don’t know, because it depends on if someone’s wanting something with melody or a traditional song or something more esoteric and ambient. If someone wants something with more traditional songwriting, I’d probably recommend A Chaos of Desire over Remnants of a Deeper Purity. Well, I know it’s certainly hard to choose a favorite child, so I won’t press further. Speaking of the catalogue though, I know you’ve often re-recorded songs over the years. For example, there are several versions of “Memory, Uncaring Friend” with different vocalists, as well as new updates of “Across a Thousand Blades,” which is kind of “the hit” isn’t it? I also remember you submitted a 2025 remix of “Within These Walls” for the No Songs Tomorrow box set I put together for Cherry Red. What drives you to revisit the body of work and update it over the years? Well, I would say with “Across a Thousand Blades,” it was that I never got the mix right and I tried adding things over the years. The mix I did for the 2020 remastered edition of Ashes in the Brittle Air at the end of the second disc is the one I finally got right, in my opinion. Across a Thousand remixes! Yeah, we didn’t really record any new parts for that one. The electric guitar on the original mix was pretty buried and then in another version it came up maybe too loud and so on. Then we started playing it live in 1996 and I replaced the bass sound since I couldn’t find the original bass sound anymore… When we started playing with Bret Helm from Audra as our singer, we were interested in capturing the sound of the band as a moment in time. Same when Athan Maroulis became our singer. Overall, there’s probably about 10-12 reworkings of older songs that have ended up on a compilation or as a b-side or something like that. We did “Memory, Uncaring Friend” in 2003 with Bret singing on top of the original track but I also re-recorded it completely in 2009 with Athan. That version had Brian Viglione from Dresden Dolls on drums, and it felt more immediate. I always thought that song could have been tighter, almost like a Gary Numan song… Overall though, we still want to keep the essence of things. There are artists like Frank Zappa for example, who entirely altered older albums, replacing drums with drum machines, and that’s not really what I’m trying to do with that. I agree with that. I’m not a fan of the George Lucas “revisionist history” thing. I’m all for alternate mixes, especially if they’re an improvement over the original, but at the same time, the original version should still be available for people who are used to it. Why deny the work exists? There’s permanence to art once it’s released and to pretend that’s not the case is frustrating and confusing, especially in the streaming era. So I like what you’ve done, putting out exclusive mixes on compilations, remixing albums for a bonus disc, and so on. As a collector, this gives me a reason to seek it out and it adds to the discography instead of replacing it. Exactly. With the new version of The Rope that’s coming out on 2CD and 2LP, I’m offering both the remastered original mix as well as a new mix I did of the album. The new mix isn’t that drastically different from the old mix. It’s just that the levels are right now that I had time to mix it. Some of the instruments that got buried before are a little louder. It’s like the Steve Wilson mixes that I’ve heard that aren’t really trying to be something new, they’re just trying to make the original sound a little bit clearer. They’ve done that with a few Bowie mixes, too. There are some complete reworkings or reimaginings of some albums that are great, and there are some so-so mixes, but the new version of Lodger is my preferred, since that was a dicey mix in the first place. However, as I said, I think there’s a certain charm to the early Blacktape records, that youthful abandon and inexperience that actually can elevate things. That said, it’s great you have all the tapes and are able to go back and make things sound the way you really wanted them to. I definitely have heard from many people that say The Rope is their favorite album and that’s the mix I did in two hours way back when. So I do have to honor that… Right, why deny it ever happened, especially since it’s out there on various formats. Yeah, and of course, with art, a listener doesn’t perceive mistakes the same way the artist might. Same thing with live performances. Sometimes I’ve come off stage thinking that a song didn’t really work, but then people come up to me and say they loved the show. You have to believe that, even if it’s not what you feel. I’ve been there more times than I can count. I’m my own worst critic on stage and if I play something even a little differently, not even necessarily a mistake, that sometimes has colored my feelings about the show, for better or for worse. Everyone’s tastes and perceptions are a little different… Yeah, I feel like as long as you didn’t get booed off stage, then it was probably a good show (laughs). Well, speaking of live shows, did you really only start playing live in 1996? Yes. I played one show in 1983 or 1984 in Florida and played a few with Walter Holland in 86-87 in California. We had an electronic band called Doppler Shift and we played a couple of shows And Blacktape’s first show was at the 1996 ProjektFest? Yes. I was talking with Pat, who I play with in his project Thanatos, about projects that have one person and how difficult it is to tour and deal with clubs every night. So we thought maybe we should do a festival in Chicago, have people come to us rather than make the bands go from city to city. This way, we could hone in our sound. So yeah, Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s first show was ProjektFest in 1996. Wow, no warm-ups—just right into the fray! Yeah! I don’t do that now. When we started touring after that, we’d do a smaller show before hitting a major city, making sure that New York City is not the first gig of the tour. I know people (myself included) who still talk about ProjektFest and how it was such a scene staple. Did you do them every year, or was it sporadic? We did 1996 and 1997 in Chicago. Those were two nights each. Then in 1998 we did one night in LA, Philly, Chicago, and New York, but they weren’t back to back, there was some gap between them as far as I remember. There were also different lineups in Los Angeles, I think Faith and the Muse and Love Spirals Downwards played on those bills since they were based in California. As for our live set in ‘96 and ‘97, I relied on Oscar to be the musical director for the band since he had played out so much in his other bands. I wasn’t experienced, so I leaned on him to help get the live band, the Remnants-era band, rehearsed properly. At a show in November 1998, we played at an art museum in Philadelphia in the afternoon and Vicki and I stayed behind to do an instrumental set while the rest of the band went to New York to set up. Vicki and I finished the set and took the train since it was a quick train ride between the two cities. Wow, that was a risky thing to do—so many things that could have gone wrong! Yeah, if we missed the train, we’d have been out of luck, but the NYC show was opening for The Creatures at Irving Plaza, so we couldn’t pass it up! We did have a backup plan, the sound guy was going to play my parts along with a backing track if I didn’t make it. But you did make it! Yeah, fortunately! I remember that the Irving Plaza stage isn’t very big and we were very cramped up in the front. Ah, classic… I’m sure there was a massive drum kit with all kinds of wild percussion up there. Right, Budgie’s set up. It was very stressful, but now it’s a good story! So after those first wave of shows, did playing live become a much bigger priority? It seems like the records were more and more spaced out from that point, which would make sense if you were focusing on the live aspect of the band. It was 1999 when we started touring more. Before that it was those festival shows really, and it was just a way to promote the band. On tour we’d end up playing goth club nights where there would be fast-paced dancing and then we’d come in and kind of slow things down for a while. If I look at the numbers, I think we did something like 134 shows total over the course of 10-12 years. It wasn’t continuous, the slowdown of releases was partially due to that, but also because running Projekt took more time, there were a lot of bands on the label, a lot of employees, and then Lisa and I had a baby, so that slowed things down even more, as you might expect. I’d seen you several times after (not counting that time we played together) but the FIRST time I saw Black Tape for a Blue Girl was at the ProjektFest in Philadelphia in 2002, and Lisa was pregnant with your son. That whole weekend was pretty incredible, I still think of it very fondly. Was that the last year of ProjektFest? No, there was one in 2007 that was smaller. It seemed people were past the point of coming to festivals. Yeah, and I imagine the label roster had grown to a much larger capacity at that point, with bands scattered across the US and beyond. You were also releasing a lot of ambient releases, branching out into shoegaze, and so on. How did your signing process evolve over the years? At this point, it was less about demo tapes and more that someone who was already on the label would recommend a band. Though I signed Mira quickly after Regina gave us a demo tape at one of our Florida shows. Bold! Yeah, same with Voltaire. We were in the van with nothing else to listen to, so we’d pop in demo tapes. I can’t remember what the last physical demo I got, but now it’s all Soundcloud links and private playlists, not even downloads. I don’t want to deal with files anymore. I admire what you built with Projekt—it was all a labor of love, and there are so many great bands I wouldn’t have heard if you didn’t spend much of your time cultivating the label. Maybe I’m romanticizing that a bit, but I think you did the right thing, but I dunno, I’m not you and couldn’t say if you’re satisfied with Blacktape’s trajectory… Honestly, if my band had had a manager in 1997 after Remnants, they would have said, “Why are you wasting your time promoting those other bands and not working your own band? Your band just sold all these records. Why aren’t you making a new album, man?” If Lycia had a manager, that manager would have been trying to get them onto a bigger label, right? The band was extremely successful, they’re touring with Type O Negative, they should be on a label where someone can put money behind them. I always thought that it would be GREAT if these bands left the label to move up to somewhere. I always saw Projekt as a starting ground, you know? Metropolis was about signing European bands and bringing them to the US market. I saw Projekt as a place to release great new bands and give them a springboard. I know that bands like Lovesliescrushing have released material on different labels, but did any of the bands successfully make the jump? It seemed like everyone stuck with Projekt, whether it be a matter of loyalty or convenience. Again, that’s a romantic notion… Yeah, it’s all hindsight now, but these bands needed a good manager who played the game knowing what the next steps are and how to get to the point you want to get to, but none of us had managers. For a period, Lycia was full-time touring, but everyone else it was their hobby. It wasn’t their full-time job. Some of the bands wanted to go from working day jobs to having a full-blown music career but it was the in-between part that they weren’t pushing for. I get it, it’s a lot of hard work and money for just a roll of the dice. Yeah, and even with Blacktape, I can look back now and Blacktape should have toured with Oscar, because he was the voice people knew and he was dramatic and charismatic on stage, but he was in Miami and he had a family and he was doing what he needed to do, so, it wasn’t possible. Well, there’s something to be said about that, then… There’s a band I used to know, who I won’t name, and they always were talking about a future where they’re selling 50,000 records. I told them to be realistic, they’re not even selling 3,000. 50,000 is not the next step, you need to take the step to 10,000, little by little. Being a successful band takes a lot of listening to others and nobody really likes that… So, continuing the Blacktape story, as the band continued, you often worked with different collaborators, like Bret Helm who we mentioned before, Michael Laird from Unto Ashes, and so on. I really adore The Scavenger Bride, which is pretty much the peak of the sound you were going for in the nineties in my opinion, still lush, very dramatic, very literary, all the things I look for in music. Then, shortly after, starting with Halo Star, you changed styles to incorporate more cabaret and steampunk influences. What inspired that shift? I think every artist has the optimistic belief that they can be like Bowie: that they can do different things and have everyone follow them on the journey, but in retrospect, I don’t think everyone can because not everyone has a wide enough audience base. There’s a lot I really like about 10 Neurotics, but I think listeners weren’t really looking for that. Well, it’s not like you didn’t hint at that sound a bit on Halo Star, and I know that sound and style was popular, at least in the NYC goth scene at the time. There was something literary and romantic about that, too, so even if it’s not my go-to genre, there’s still times where that sound can hit the spot. Anyway, did the folks you were working with go on the journey with you as well, aside from Athan? Well, I usually have a song written and then I bring in people to play on it. We did that with The Scavenger Bride, where Michael Laird would come in and add textures, and in other cases, sometimes the percussion would drive the song more, but the real basis of the song would exist before I brought anyone else in. The secret is bringing in interesting musicians who can work within that structure. “Inch Worm” actually was written before Halo Star, but I couldn’t figure out the song until much later. The same is true with “the Turbulence and the Torment” from This Lush Garden Within, which was recorded during A Chaos of Desire. With 10 Neurotics, I worked with Brian Viglione. I was looking for a drummer, despite not caring much for drummers generally, but the music asked for that. I think drummers do a bit too much and are a bit too busy. My favorite drummer is Steve Jansen from Japan since he doesn’t overplay, he does what’s needed to create the right mood. So, working with Brian, he was a really great musician who understood my musical language and was able to shape the song and not overdo it, unless that was required. This is weird, but ultimately, how you publicize the record does stick in people’s head for how they perceive the record. I think 10 Neurotics was probably over-publicized in one direction. You know, if the one sheet had been written differently, I think people would have given it more of a shot and perceived it differently. It’s kind of like what you put in the movie trailer has a lot to do with how people think your movie’s going to be. Sometimes that’s right. Sometimes it’s not. One of the tracks is a steampunk-mixed-with-Philip-Glass thing. We also worked with Lucas Lanthier from Cinema Strange. Then there’s a few tracks in the middle where Nicki Jane sings. As you said, with Halo Star, I think that record reflected the sound of us playing in clubs. The songs are a bit more upbeat. There was a larger gap between those two, and then an even bigger gap between 10 Neurotics and These Fleeting Moments, where it seemed you went back to a more classic sound. What happened during those years? I spent time writing Rye in 2012 and then moved to Portland in 2013. I wanted to write another book, but instead I decided to spend time acclimating to Portland. There was an EP called Bike Shop in 2016 that Michael Plaster from Soul Whirling Somewhere sings. These were songs I had written on guitar, I really loved that it was acoustic and a very coherent, but different, feeling. I wish more people had heard it because Soul Whirling Somewhere hadn’t done an album in 18 years or something like that. I wrote lyrics to fit Michael’s personality, almost like he was a character in the story. I crowdfunded that EP and the delays in manufacturing pushed it close to the release of These Fleeting Moments. That album was intentionally going back more to the Remnants-ish sound. Oscar had retired from music at that point, so he hadn’t sung on anything since As One Aflame Laid Bare By Desire. I asked if he would want to sing on it. He then suggested that Danielle, his daughter, could sing the female vocal parts. It worked out quite well. I don’t quite know how many people have been in Black Tape for a Blue Girl over the years. It’s got to be in the 40-50 people range, you know, between collaborators and vocalists. With a few exceptions, I generally liked having singers that were exclusively in my band and not guests from another band like This Mortal Coil. Bike Shop (EP) by Black Tape For A Blue Girl Right, I suppose Athan and Oscar had been in previous bands but those bands had broken up by the time they joined Blacktape. I guess Bret from Audra is the exception to that rule, though Audra took some time off when he was in the band. Yeah I guess I sort of contradicted myself here. On the most recent album, I had Jon DeRosa who’s band is Aarktica as well as his own solo work. Audra were one of the bands who we met early on because they opened up for us in Austin. Audra had two albums on Projekt and everything worked well on the Blacktape albums Bret sang on; he fit perfectly with the sound. We recorded the vocals for The Scavenger Bride at Steve Roach’s studio, if I remember correctly. Athan lived in Brooklyn, near where I lived, so it made it easy to work with him around that time. I feel like I saw the band with Bret three times: ProjektFest, a show at Downtime where the Mirror Reveals opened when I just moved to the city, and a show a little later when local friends The Hunt and Martial Canterel played. I think that was at Europa, that old dance club turned venue. I really liked that place, as weird as it was… Was that the club in Greenpoint? I have a recording of that show. I’ll have to dig it out and transfer it someday. Well you’ve been releasing a lot of work-in-progress mixes and live shows as part of the subscriber project, right? Perhaps it’s time to put that one up! Yeah, true, I did put up a live video of a whole show from 1998 on YouTube and some audio here and there, one from the 2002 festival that I sang, which is relatively rare. Let’s talk about the last three albums! There have been three Blacktape albums that I recorded since moving to Portland in 2013. These Fleeting Moments, To Touch the Milky Way, and The Cleft Serpent. The Cleft Serpent was the first album with only three band members. There are no instrumentals and all the songs feature male vocals. It really was an album that was written for characters: the Cleft Serpent and the Trickster. I’d known Jon, the vocalist on the album, since New York. He opened for a lot of Projekt bands/shows dating back to when he was 16-17—something like that. We worked on a track together in 2020 that was a reworking of the Aarktica track “Eating Rose Petals.” It was an experiment to see how we’d work together and it went incredibly smoothly. He understands Blacktape since he’s known the band since he was young. I used the same process as always where I recorded the vocal melody and lyrics and sent it to Jon to perform, it’s all predetermined. He was able to record it in a studio in LA without me, which I’d never done before. He gave me four takes so I could pick between the different emotions he’s put into it. For him, some of the lyrics were more dramatic than what he’s used to singing. Once he started thinking about it as a character, rather than as his own authentic feeling, he got into what I was writing for him…. But that’s sort of the Blacktape style, isn’t it? There are always characters. Something like “The Lie Which Refuses to Die” or “Tell Me You’ve Taken Another” are character-driven. It’s great that Jon gets that and is able to bring that to the table and that you still have that structure. That was always the plan. When I had seen Oscar’s original band, I knew that I could write a song with that much drama in it because he had the power that Bowie or Freddy Mercury or Marc Almond had. Oscar, or Athan, or Jon could give the songs what I needed to make them work. Yeah, there’s so much of that kitchen sink drama there, like Scott Walker had as well. Right. Marc Almond’s Torment & Toreros and Mother Fist And Her Five Daughters were early touchstones. You know: sad people who fucked up their lives and lost everything yet are blaming others for the things they’ve fucked up. Maybe if someone was writing about their own life, they would walk back certain things or not sound as proud about what they messed up, but if someone else is singing, I feel like we can take that as far as it needs to go. With The Cleft Serpent, I love the cohesiveness of just three people in the band. The songs all feel like one mood. So what are you working on now? What’s next for Blacktape? I know you’ve been working on some solo material and other projects as well as reissues, but is there any new music in progress? No, I haven’t been working on anything for Blacktape. I just released an electronic drone album called The Width of Shadows and I’m also working on another drone album in collaboration with Arin, a Projekt artist in Norway. Honestly, the process of recording makes me so annoyed. It’s so tedious. I figure it takes 400 hours to record a Blacktape album because I’m compulsive and strive for perfection that no one can hear. It drives me nuts to be like that. I hope one day I’ll be able to do a Blacktape album in two weeks so I’m not so obsessed about everything. I did a different project called Nova Cat Purring Sounds where I took my kitty’s purring, and some of it is just purrs and some of it is accompanied by ambient music. I must mention that Nova has passed away since then. But it was so easy to make and very therapeutic. It was pleasant to put together this album in a week or two. With the most recent electronic album, I tried to use the same process and not be so obsessive. It’s interesting, too, because, like I said earlier, there’s something to be said about making mistakes in art. Mistakes can be interpreted by others as passion, and in the end, who’s right? The one who created it, or the one who has a connection to the work once it’s out. released? Purring Cat for Sleep, Study & Relaxation (ASMR) by Nova Cat Purring Sounds Well that also ties in to the punk/post-punk scene that we all come from. Not that Blacktape is punk by definition, but there’s that DIY spirit that runs through your work. That said, making an ambient record out of cat purrs is pretty punk in a way! I sincerely mean that. Well, you know, I started listening to music in 1976 or so, and although I wasn’t listening to punk bands at the time, the whole punk idea to me is definitely in there in the sense that I started a record label to release music, built up a fan base, and didn’t wait for somebody’s permission to do that thing. I have lived the last 30-35 years with Projekt helping people put out their music and there’s a wide variety of releases on the label. There are maybe 650 releases on the label now and it’s pretty great being able to survive in the music industry. So I mean it in the Punk DIY aesthetic, not waiting for permission. Just do it! I don’t really know when I will make another Blacktape for a Blue Girl record, it’s not on my mind right now, but I am grateful for everything the label has done, all the support people have given me and the bands, and everything I’ve been able to do along the way. Thanks for talking, it was great catching up! § Follow Black Tape for a Blue Girl Linktree Bandcamp Facebook Instagram Website Twitter The post Within These Walls — An Interview with Sam Rosenthal of Black Tape For a Blue Girl appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.excerpt: Woe is me, woe is you Woe consumes both us two Heartbreak has a cruel invertibility: the person who opens the wound can remain the person we most want to close it. After love breaks, desire divides against itself. One half wishes for a return, for the old tenderness to be restored and the damage somehow withdrawn; the other wants the absent lover to wake inside the same pain, because understanding can feel incomplete until it is physical. Reconciliation and retribution begin to share a border. “
items.body: Woe is me, woe is you Woe consumes both us two Heartbreak has a cruel invertibility: the person who opens the wound can remain the person we most want to close it. After love breaks, desire divides against itself. One half wishes for a return, for the old tenderness to be restored and the damage somehow withdrawn; the other wants the absent lover to wake inside the same pain, because understanding can feel incomplete until it is physical. Reconciliation and retribution begin to share a border. “Come back” and “suffer as I have” become rival versions of the same plea: see what happened to me. That double wish supplies the emotional engine of DECEITS’ latest single, One Day You’ll Hurt As Much As Me. Released on March 25th, the song is the Los Angeles duo’s first official release with Get Better Records. It now receives a brilliantly shot video directed by Raquel Rojas, who gives its divided feelings a physical route through memory, childhood, and the disappearing view from a train window. A thick, melodic bass figure takes the first step, with Francisco Saenz’s drums answering in a cymbal splash before a dance-minded hi-hat locks the song into motion. Above them, a sustained guitar riff trembles around its melody. Kevin Moreno sings with a Robert Smith-like romantic ache, drawing out the opening supplications before compressing the repeated phrase about silent suffering into a quick, addictive cadence. The Cure resemblance lives in the emotional pitch, while DECEITS propel the song with the rapid, bass-led momentum of faster Cure songs such as “Primary,” allowing grief to pass through the body rather than remain fixed as a confessional dirge. Among the duo’s recordings to date, it ranks as one of their strongest: romantic post-punk with real velocity and a chorus made for a crowded room. Moreno’s lyrics keep the song’s lover in incompatible roles: desired comforter, departing betrayer, and imagined fellow sufferer. He asks for closeness and a cure, then for abandonment and emotional erasure, as though every available exit must be tested. “Woe is me, woe is you” is the song’s plainest and most revealing line, making misery reciprocal before the title turns that symmetry into a future verdict. The wish carries spite, but also a bruised faith in recognition: someday, perhaps, the other person will feel enough to understand. The video’s director Raquel Rojas gives that emotional bargain a coastal route. Moreno and Saenz ride an Amtrak car visited—or perhaps accompanied—by Gustavo Alexander Moreno and Logan Martínez as their childhood counterparts. Present-day close-ups dissolve into grainy footage of the children on station platforms and at the beach, building in the sand and racing beside the water as the train follows the Pacific. The carriage becomes a place where youth and adulthood can share seats without quite seeing one another. Performance scenes place the duo inside a chain-link pedestrian overpass and beside the tracks, with the bright coast visible beyond the enclosure. Past and present seem briefly reversible, yet the edits never grant them a clean reunion; each age slips over the other like damaged film. Travel supplies movement without escape. By the closing views from the window, the landscape is retreating too quickly to hold, leaving the video’s central question unresolved: were those earlier days genuinely easier, or has distance made them kinder than they were? Watch the video for “One Day You’ll Hurt As Much As Me” below: Since forming in 2021, longtime friends Moreno (vocals and instruments) and Saenz (drums and percussion) have built DECEITS from the ground up. The duo self-released its catalog, accumulated millions of streams, sold out tours, and produced vinyl pressings that disappeared almost as soon as they became available. The partnership with Get Better Records marks a significant turn in that history while preserving the fiercely independent spirit that brought them this far. DECEITS draw upon the color, rhythm, and emotional directness of the Spanish-language music they grew up with, shaping a warmer and more kinetic form of post-punk. Their all-analog live setup and punk beginnings lend each set a degree of instability: arrangements breathe, tempos flex, and no two performances land exactly the same way. That combination of romantic intensity and physical force has earned the band an international following throughout the dark alternative underground. The duo has appeared on bills with She Past Away, She Wants Revenge, New Order, and Anka Huwe of Xmal Deutschland. On November 14th, DECEITS will perform at Darker Waves Festival in Huntington Beach alongside Morrissey, The Smashing Pumpkins, Simple Minds, Gary Numan, The Psychedelic Furs, The Damned, and more. Listen to “One Day You’ll Hurt As Much As Me” below and order the single through here. One Day You’ll Hurt As Much As Me by DECEITS DECEITS will carry the anguish and velocity of “One Day You’ll Hurt As Much As Me” across the United States this fall on the Hurt As Much As Me Tour 2026. Beginning September 24th at Slowdown in Omaha, the run crosses the Midwest, Northeast, and South with Computer Kill before joining Haunt Me for two Florida dates. DECEITS then return to California for an appearance at The Roxy Theatre with Mind’s Eye and Camp Blu, an Ocean Beach show with Christian Death, and a as mentioned before, concluding with a performance at Darker Waves Festival in Huntington Beach. Tickets and further information can be found through the band’s Linktree and official shows page. items.excerpt: Charm is one of the stranger forms of social currency, because its value depends on everybody agreeing, for a moment, to overlook the arithmetic. items.body: Charm is one of the stranger forms of social currency, because its value depends on everybody agreeing, for a moment, to overlook the arithmetic. The charmer gets the favour, the second chance; somebody else absorbs the cost. On It Always Comes to Me, the final advance single from Black Marble’s Life in Small Spaces, Chris Stewart studies that transaction with the detached curiosity of someone watching a confidence game unfold across a crowded room. “It Always Comes to Me is about a cool, calm, collected person who seems to always be able to get away with things other people can’t, either by charm or deceit,” says Stewart. “Like a modern version of The Kinks’ Dedicated Follower of Fashion, the song doesn’t explicitly advocate for or condemn this kind of behaviour, but takes a birds eye view of it as the protagonist moves through the world. Ultimately, it leaves it up to the listener to judge for themselves. The subject of the song seems to be having fun but can it last? And how much does our judgement really matter either way?” Stewart’s subject has mistaken self-preservation for a philosophy, treating other people as scenery in a private campaign of convenience…yet each successful escape removes another beam from the structure holding a person among others. Isolation is built one victory at a time. Bass and guitar carry more weight here than Black Marble’s older walls of synthesizers, giving the song the warmth of musicians occupying shared space. Stewart has described the album’s new guitar language as an attempt to “create this chime-y hypnotic quality. Like a radio dial that is between two stations.” The image suits a record concerned with people caught between versions of themselves, transmitting confidence while a less flattering signal bleeds through. Claes Nordwall’s video places Stewart in New York, drifting through subways, bridges, basketball courts, and pool halls with an ease that mirrors the song’s central figure. “I was drawn to the idea of a character moving through the modern world on his own timeline,” says Nordwall. “While everything around him races forward, he remains quietly rooted in who he is. I was inspired by Chris’s ideas behind the album which made me think of the dry stoicism of Aki Kaurismäki’s films. I wanted to make something that celebrates resilience, character and the beauty of refusing to chase the next thing.” The result is a tender snapshot of modern day city life in the Big Apple, which, ironically, feels timeless, as if filmed thirty years ago. The irony remains unresolved. A person moving at his own pace may be independent, deluded, enviable, or alone. Stewart leaves the verdict open, while the song quietly asks what remains when getting away with everything finally means having nobody left to fool. Watch the video for It Always Comes to Me below: Life in Small Spaces is out August 21st on Sacred Bones. Pre-order here. items.body: 2026.08.19 シューベルトのピアノ曲を聴いてみたい。でも、作品が多くて、どこから聴けばいいのかわからない……そんな人に向けて、シューベルトのピアノ曲全曲演奏に取り組むピアニスト・佐藤卓史さんに、「まず聴いてほしい3曲」を教えてもらいました。 2007年の第11回シューベルト国際ピアノコンクールで優勝し、2014年から「シューベルト・ツィクルス」としてピアノ曲全曲演奏に取り組む佐藤さん。シューベルトのピアノ曲にはどんな作品があり、最初の一歩には何を選べばいいのでしょうか。 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る ※本記事はポッドキャスト番組『ONTOMO Radio』で語られた内容を再構成しています。 佐藤卓史（さとう・たかし） 第11回シューベルト国際コンクールでの優勝と、その後の世界的な演奏活動を通して“現代随一のシューベルト弾き”の名声を確立。展開中のライフワークプロジェクト「佐藤卓史シューベルトツィクルス」では、未完成作品の補筆を含む前人未踏のシューベルトのピアノ曲全曲演奏に取り組み、注目を集めている。 秋田市生まれ。高校在学中に日本音楽コンクールで優勝。東京藝術大学を首席で卒業後渡欧、ハノーファー音楽演劇大学、ウィーン国立音楽大学で研鑽を積む。その間、ミュンヘンARD国際コンクール特別賞、シューベルト国際コンクール第1位、シドニー国際コンクール第4位・ショパン特別賞、エリザベート王妃国際コンクール入賞、カントゥ国際コンクール第1位、メンデルスゾーン国際コンクール最高位など受賞多数。ウィーン楽友協会をはじめとする欧州各地のコンサートホールに出演のほか、2011年にはシリア・ダマスカスのダール・アル・アサド文化芸術劇場でソロリサイタルを開催。 NHK交響楽団、東京交響楽団、日本フィルハーモニー交響楽団、山形交響楽団、仙台フィルハーモニー管弦楽団、神奈川フィルハーモニー管弦楽団、大阪交響楽団、広島交響楽団、ベルギー国立管弦楽団など内外のオーケストラと多数共演。「トリオ・ジャパン」（with石田泰尚・西谷牧人）、「トリオ・スペリオール」（with泉原隆志・上森祥平）各メンバーを務めるなど、アンサンブルピアニストとしての活躍は特に知られており、著名アーティストから絶え間ない共演オファーが寄せられ続けている。 近年は作編曲の分野でも活動を本格化させるほか、放送・配信・執筆・レクチャーなど幅広いフィールドで音楽の“楽しさ”と“奥深さ”を伝える活動に力を注いでいる。 www.takashi-sato.jp シューベルトのピアノ曲は大きく分けて3つ ——まず、シューベルトのピアノ曲には、どのような作品があるのでしょうか？ 佐藤 曲の数は、どう数えるかによって変わってくるのですが、ざっくり大きなジャンルとして3つあります。1つはピアノ・ソナタ、2つ目が「性格小品（キャラクター・ピース）」と呼ばれるもの、そして3つ目が舞曲です。 ソナタは、同じ時代に、同じウィーンにいた26歳上のベートーヴェンを尊敬し畏怖の念すらあったので、それに対して、自分はどういうソナタを書いていこうかと模索しチャレンジしていたジャンルです。 性格小品には、8曲の《即興曲》と6曲からなる《楽興の時》があります。シューベルトのピアノ曲全体からすると数はそれほど多くありませんが、聴くにも弾くにも昔から親しまれているジャンルです。 そして舞曲。ここれは実用的な目的、つまり仲間うちのダンスパーティーなどで踊るための伴奏として作られました。当時のウィーンで流行っていたので、生前にも出版社からいくつもの曲集が出されています。現在見つかっているだけでも数百曲あると言われています。 その1：《楽興の時》D780〜抒情的な短い曲を気軽に楽しむ ——それでは、シューベルトのピアノ曲を初めて聴く人に向けて、おすすめを3曲挙げていただけますか？ 佐藤 「超入門」ということなので、まずは聴きやすい《楽興の時》D780という性格小品をおすすめします。 6曲からなる曲集ですが、全部聴いても20数分ほど。もちろん通して聴いてもいいですし、1曲ずつ抜き出して聴いても、それぞれ違った印象があって楽しめます。自分の時間に合わせて、「今日はこの1曲だけ」と聴けるのもいいところですね。 優しさ、抒情性、それからポエティックな感じが強いので、そういうところを味わいながら聴くと、シューベルトの世界に入っていけるのでは。情景を思い浮かべながら、風が吹いてきた、鳥の歌声が聴こえるといった想像を膨らませるのも楽しいと思います。 《楽興の時》を含む、佐藤卓史さんの第11回シューベルト国際ピアノコンクール優勝記念レコーディング ——第3番は特に有名で、ラジオのテーマ曲や給食の音楽になっていましたね。 佐藤 古くから全世界的に親しまれているので、録音をコレクションして、テンポや繰り返しの有無などを比較して聴き進めてもおもしろいかもしれません。 ——ちなみに、シューベルト好きの佐藤さん、思い出の録音はありますか？ 佐藤 ラドゥ・ルプー、あるいはアンドラーシュ・シフの録音なんかも、すごく好きでした。古いものだと、ヴィルヘルム・バックハウスやルドルフ・ゼルキン。古い時代の人たちのシューベルトの解釈って、現代の人とはまたちょっと違った、さっぱりしてるというか、サクサクと音楽が進んでいって、ちょっとドライな感じ。そういう演奏も、爽やかで、逆に味わい深い感じもありますね。 ラドゥ・ルプーとアンドラーシュ・シフの演奏 その2：1969年に発見された“謎の曲”《グラーツ幻想曲》を聴く ——では、2曲目は？ 佐藤 今度は、ちょっと珍しい曲を挙げたいと思います。《グラーツ幻想曲》です。 この曲は、なんと1969年に新たに発見されるまで存在が知られていなかった作品です。シューベルトの友人ヒュッテンブレンナーの遺品の中から見つかりました。 発見された当初は、「本当にシューベルトが書いたのか」と思われるほど新しい響きを持っていて、真贋をめぐる論争もあったそうです。それほど変わった魅力のある曲なんですね。 ——そんな「幻の作品」が、今では聴けるようになっているんですね。 佐藤 作曲年代もわかっていないのですが。 ——ドイチュ番号のD605Aというのは、だいたいその時期という意味ではないのですね？ 佐藤 そうなんです。D605の未完の幻想曲と同じようなスタイルの曲ということで並べておいたというくらいだと思います。 昔から幻想曲はあるんですが、要するに即興的にどんどんセクションが脈絡なく並べられていくようなスタイルの曲です。例えばシューベルトの《さすらい幻想曲》は、1つのモチーフに基づいて、もう少し緻密に組み立てられている幻想曲なんですが、この《グラーツ幻想曲》はそうではない。いろいろなセクションが次々に現れて、それぞれのキャラクターがとてもはっきりしている。まるで「いろんな夢の国を旅行している」ような楽しい曲で、美しい響きもたくさんある。 ものすごく緻密に計算して組み立てたというより、その場で思いついたフレッシュなアイデアが次々と楽譜になっているような魅力があります。 シューベルト：《グラーツ幻想曲》 その3：最後は大作に挑戦！「ピアノ・ソナタ第21番」D 960 佐藤 3つ目には、シューベルトが非常に力を入れて取り組んだソナタというジャンルを聴いていただきたいと思います。 シューベルトの完成したソナタは長いものが多く、聴き通すにはある程度の体力も必要です。でも、どのソナタも本当に素晴らしい。その中から1曲だけ挙げるとしたら、最後の番号が付いたD 960、一般に「ピアノ・ソナタ第21番」と呼ばれている作品です。 演奏時間は約40分。4楽章からなる大作のソナタで、シューベルトが最晩年に書いた作品です。 ——40分となると、《楽興の時》からはかなりハードルが上がりますね。 佐藤 シューベルトが最後に書いた作品です。 ——亡くなるのが11月19日で、最後のソナタ3曲が書かれたのが9月とされていたようですが、本当でしょうか？ 佐藤 昔は、9月の数週間で3曲のソナタを一気に書いたんだ、という話があったのですが、最近はさすがにそれはないだろうと言われていて、春ぐらいから構想したものが、9月頃完成したんじゃないかと。 それにしたってすごい早さですよね。 この曲には、シューベルトの生きてきた人生の集大成のようなものが、メッセージとして残されているように感じます。とても叙情的ですし、特に第2楽章には、すごく孤独な感じの歌が続いていくところがあって、本当に心に染みるような感動があります。そして全曲を通して聴いていくと、最後には魂が救済されていくような、とてもカタルシスのある体験になると思います。 シューベルト：ピアノ・ソナタ第21番D 960 シューベルトのピアノ曲を弾いてみたい人へのおすすめ3曲はこちら 演奏会情報 佐藤卓史シューベルトツィクルス第24回 「4手のための序曲 ―オペラの夢―」 日時： 2026年9月13日（日）14：00開演 会場： 音楽の友ホール 出演： 佐藤卓史、尾崎未空（ピアノ） 曲目： シューベルト／イタリア風序曲 ニ長調 D592、歌劇《アルフォンソとエストレッラ》序曲 D773、英雄的大行進曲 D885、イタリア風序曲 ハ長調 D597、歌劇《フィエラブラス》序曲 D798、エロルドの歌劇《マリー》の主題による8つの変奏曲 D908 詳しくはこちら 「佐藤卓史シューベルトツィクルス」企画第24回。今回のサブタイトルは「オペラの夢」。上記2つの代表作《アルフォンソ》《フィエラブラス》の序曲は、シューベルト自身がピアノ連弾用に編曲している。これが今回のメインで、加えて19歳のときにロッシーニの《幸福な錯覚》の上演を聴き、そのイタリア風の明るい響きに影響されて書いたという2曲の「イタリア風序曲」（やはり作曲者自身による連弾版）、またケルントナートーア劇場のコレペティトーア時代にオペラの挿入曲を書いていた作曲家エロルドのオペラ《マリー》の主題による変奏曲など、シューベルトのオペラとの関わりに焦点を当てたプログラムを取り上げる。 連弾で共演する尾崎未空はミュンヘン在住のピアニストで、日本ではPTNA特級グランプリでおなじみのほか、国際的に活躍中。2人だけでの共演は今回が初めて。 ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら シューベルトに関する記事一覧 シューベルトに関する書籍

items.excerpt: 2026.08.19 8月21日（金）にサントリーホールで特級ファイナル開催、YouTubeライブで生中継 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る ピティナ・ピアノコンペティションは、全日本ピアノ指導者協会（ピティナ）が主催する日本最大規模のピアノコンクール。そのソロ部門における最高峰である「特級」は、課題や日程の設計において「もっとも国際コンクールに近い国内コンクール」を標榜している。これまで阪田知樹、角野隼斗、亀井聖矢、進藤実優、山縣美季、桑原志織、鈴木愛美など、錚々たるピアニストたちがこの「特級」から世界へ羽ばたいていった。 昨年からセミファイナルに室内楽審査が導入され、一流の共演者とのアンサンブルを通して、ソリストとしての資質だけでなく、音楽を深く理解し響き合う力も問われるようになった「特級」。聴衆の開拓にも努め、聴衆賞の創設やライブ配信の早期実現など、絶えざる進化を続けてきた。 今年、半世紀の歴史を経て記念すべき
items.body: 2026.08.19 8月21日（金）にサントリーホールで特級ファイナル開催、YouTubeライブで生中継 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る ピティナ・ピアノコンペティションは、全日本ピアノ指導者協会（ピティナ）が主催する日本最大規模のピアノコンクール。そのソロ部門における最高峰である「特級」は、課題や日程の設計において「もっとも国際コンクールに近い国内コンクール」を標榜している。これまで阪田知樹、角野隼斗、亀井聖矢、進藤実優、山縣美季、桑原志織、鈴木愛美など、錚々たるピアニストたちがこの「特級」から世界へ羽ばたいていった。 昨年からセミファイナルに室内楽審査が導入され、一流の共演者とのアンサンブルを通して、ソリストとしての資質だけでなく、音楽を深く理解し響き合う力も問われるようになった「特級」。聴衆の開拓にも努め、聴衆賞の創設やライブ配信の早期実現など、絶えざる進化を続けてきた。 今年、半世紀の歴史を経て記念すべき第50回を迎える。このたび決定したファイナリストは、以下の4名だ。 第50回ピティナ・ピアノコンペティション特級ファイナリスト4名とファイナルでの曲目 左上：三井 柚乃（みつい・ゆの／昭和音楽大学附属ピアノアートアカデミー在籍）、ラフマニノフ：ピアノ協奏曲第2番 右上：沢田 蒼梧（さわだ・そうご／名古屋大学医学部医学科卒業）、チャイコフスキー：ピアノ協奏曲第1番 左下：山﨑 夢叶（やまざき・ゆうと／東京藝術大学4年）、ベートーヴェン：ピアノ協奏曲第3番 右下：西山 響貴（にしやま・ひびき／桐朋学園大学院大学1年）、ショパン：ピアノ協奏曲第2番 「特級ファイナル」は8月21日にサントリーホールで開催され、ファイナリスト4名が太田弦（指揮）日本フィルハーモニー交響楽団というえりすぐりの共演者と、ピアノ協奏曲を披露する。 コンクールでありながら、サントリーホールという最高の音響で俊英の演奏が楽しめる、貴重な機会だ。ライブ配信も行なわれるので、ぜひ次代を担うピアニストたちの演奏に耳を傾け、自身の感性に合うピアニストを見つけ、未来へ向けて応援したい。 第50回ピティナ・ピアノコンペティション 特級ファイナルが生中継される YouTubeチャンネル

items.album: 星野太｜古田徹也『懐疑論』
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 発行：中央公論新社 発行日：2026/02/25 発行元ウェブサイト：https://www.chuko.co.jp/shinsho/2026/02/102894.html 日常生活のなかで当たり前とされている「何か」を疑うことは、ひとが自分でものを考え始めるための第一歩であると言ってよい。そして、伝統的に哲学と呼ばれてきた営みは、わたしたちが所与の事実とみなしている現実を根本から疑うことを、ときにみずからの務めとみなしてきた。日々の教育や就労の現場でも、わたしたちが「何となく」従っているルールやシステムを疑うことは──それが現状の具体的な「改善」をめざすかぎりにおいて──奨励されることのほうが多いだろう。 このように、わたしたちの日常生活とも無縁ではない「懐疑」だが、本書はその哲学的起源を古代ギリシアの諸流派に即して跡づける。本書前半では、紀元前5世紀の「最初のソフィスト」プロタゴラスをはじめとする人々の思想を概観しつつ（第1章）、紀元前1世紀に勃興した「ピュロン主義」という古代懐疑主義の立場が紹介される（第2章）。そのうえで後半では、モンテーニュやデカルトに代表される近代以降の懐疑
items.body: 発行：中央公論新社 発行日：2026/02/25 発行元ウェブサイト：https://www.chuko.co.jp/shinsho/2026/02/102894.html 日常生活のなかで当たり前とされている「何か」を疑うことは、ひとが自分でものを考え始めるための第一歩であると言ってよい。そして、伝統的に哲学と呼ばれてきた営みは、わたしたちが所与の事実とみなしている現実を根本から疑うことを、ときにみずからの務めとみなしてきた。日々の教育や就労の現場でも、わたしたちが「何となく」従っているルールやシステムを疑うことは──それが現状の具体的な「改善」をめざすかぎりにおいて──奨励されることのほうが多いだろう。 このように、わたしたちの日常生活とも無縁ではない「懐疑」だが、本書はその哲学的起源を古代ギリシアの諸流派に即して跡づける。本書前半では、紀元前5世紀の「最初のソフィスト」プロタゴラスをはじめとする人々の思想を概観しつつ（第1章）、紀元前1世紀に勃興した「ピュロン主義」という古代懐疑主義の立場が紹介される（第2章）。そのうえで後半では、モンテーニュやデカルトに代表される近代以降の懐疑論の姿をたどり（第3章）、著者の専門であるウィトゲンシュタインやカヴェルの議論に即して、近代的な懐疑論への批判を行なう（第4章）。 以上のようにまとめると、本書は西洋哲学における懐疑論の歴史を堅実にたどった（だけの）本のように思われるかもしれない。だがむしろ本書の読みどころは、ピュロン主義に代表される「古代懐疑主義」と、近代以降に勃興した「懐疑論」をあえて強く対照させることで、前者の意義を再発見するくだりにある。以下にその議論のポイントを抽出してみよう。 まず、著者が指摘する近代的な「懐疑論」の問題点はどこにあるのか。例えば、みずからの思惟（＝コギト）以外のすべての存在を疑ったデカルトしかり、わたしたちが身を置く世界の大部分を疑う立場は、「外界の存在全体を疑わしいものとする法外な懐疑論」（142頁）を出現させるにいたった。事実、近代以降の哲学において主流となったのは、この「全面的懐疑論」──あるいは、それをやや弱めた「局所的懐疑論」──であった。しかしながら、かつてウィトゲンシュタインが指摘したように、これらの懐疑論が抱える最大の問題は、われわれが共有する「世界像」や「生活世界」といった足場そのものを懐疑の穴に投げ込んでいる点にある。あるいはカヴェルに即して著者が書くように、「近代的な懐疑論者は、我々の生活形式にただ乗り・・・・しながら、その外部に──ひいては、この世界の外部に──出ることを欲する。それは、共有された基本的な生活形式を維持する責任を自分だけ放棄する振る舞いにほかならない」（191-192頁）。 平たく言いかえれば、こうした無責任な懐疑論は──次の「 」内は本書からの引用ではなく、あくまで評者の印象だが──いくぶん「子どもじみた」懐疑だということになろう。これに対して、より「大人びた」懐疑を展開した人々こそ、古代懐疑主義とその継承者たちである、と著者は考える。事実ピュロン主義者たちの方法は（1）絶対的な真実に到達できるという独断論と、（2）そのような真実は把握できないという否定論のいずれにも与することなく、（3）あくまで探究を継続するという前提のもと、目の前の議論を「判断保留」に導くことにあった。ピュロン主義者の目的は、この判断保留により人々を心の平穏（＝アタラクシア）へと導くことであって、その相手を「論破」することにはまったくなかった。むしろそれは、絶対的な真理を訪ね求めずにはいられない人々への一種の「治療」行為に相当したのである（彼らの多くは医師であった）。 むろん、こうした古代懐疑主義にも問題がないわけではない。というのも、この立場をつきつめると、法律・慣習・伝統といった規範に従うことが推奨されることになり、結局は「現状維持」に与することを避けられないからである。本書では、古代懐疑主義がもつ、そうした保守的な性格についても抜かりなく指摘されている。 ここまでの内容からも推察されるように、本書は陰謀論に代表される、現代の「無責任な懐疑」に対する処方箋という一面がある（第5章）。陰謀論者は自分が置かれた現実を構成する「何か」を疑って事足れりとする──そして、そのことを通じて独善的な満足を得る──わけだが、このような懐疑には端的に言って「責任」が不在なのである。ひるがえって、本書が紹介する古代懐疑主義の立場に立てば、われわれはみずからの懐疑から出発して、他者との対話に基づいたより建設的な「生活世界」の構築に努めていくべきだ、ということになろう。ひとはときに「そもそも……」というかたちで大きな懐疑を投げかける。もちろん、うまくいけばそれが大きな変革につながることもあるだろう。だがそのような問いが、当該の議論を可能にするコストを他者に転嫁していないだろうか、ということは考えてみてもよいはずだ。本書が光を当てる古代懐疑主義のエートスは、成熟した社会を復権するためのひとつの手がかりであるように思われる。 執筆日：2026/07/31（金）

items.excerpt: 会期：2026/06/12～2026/07/12 会場：TAV GALLERY［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://tavgallery.com/kentacobayashi/ 西麻布のTAV GALLERYで小林健太の個展「“TOKYO”」が開催された。小林は「#smudge」シリーズで、デジタル写真にフィジカルな指の触覚感や運動のイメージを導入し、写真というメディアの視覚性を拡張する作家として知られる。本展ではリコーによる反立体のインクジェット技術「StareReap（ステアリープ）」を用いたシリーズなどのほか、新作「“TOKYO”」のプリント3点と同シリーズが収められたクリアファイルを見ることができた。 「“TOKYO”」展［筆者撮影］ 4センチ幅ほどの亜鉛メッキ鋼板で囲まれたプリントを、分厚いアクリルブロックを重ねたものと一瞬見紛う。充満した空間を錯視させる額装も、参照源から擬似的な画面を生成するAI写真の展示に適しているように見える。 東京という都市のイメージをAIで出力したという本作は、多くが路上の景色を示している。白黒の作品だが、プリントでは紫色を帯びた黒が艶めいて美し
items.body: 会期：2026/06/12～2026/07/12 会場：TAV GALLERY［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://tavgallery.com/kentacobayashi/ 西麻布のTAV GALLERYで小林健太の個展「“TOKYO”」が開催された。小林は「#smudge」シリーズで、デジタル写真にフィジカルな指の触覚感や運動のイメージを導入し、写真というメディアの視覚性を拡張する作家として知られる。本展ではリコーによる反立体のインクジェット技術「StareReap（ステアリープ）」を用いたシリーズなどのほか、新作「“TOKYO”」のプリント3点と同シリーズが収められたクリアファイルを見ることができた。 「“TOKYO”」展［筆者撮影］ 4センチ幅ほどの亜鉛メッキ鋼板で囲まれたプリントを、分厚いアクリルブロックを重ねたものと一瞬見紛う。充満した空間を錯視させる額装も、参照源から擬似的な画面を生成するAI写真の展示に適しているように見える。 東京という都市のイメージをAIで出力したという本作は、多くが路上の景色を示している。白黒の作品だが、プリントでは紫色を帯びた黒が艶めいて美しい。3つ並ぶ信号のライトは正円でなく、車のサイドミラーのような弧を描いている。ビル群の隙間には日本列島のシルエットが浮かぶなど、人為的な解釈では起こりづらいフォルムや観念的な像が見て取れる。 「“TOKYO”」展［筆者撮影］ 本作の参照源には、デプスマップと呼ばれる被写体とカメラとの距離を画像内の深度情報として数値化するデータが用いられている。デプスマップは画像として書き出されるとき、被写体を立体的にシルエット化したようなグレースケールの像として現われる。深度値に変換がかかっているものの、「“TOKYO”」シリーズにおいて、この特徴はほとんどそのままの見え方で残されている。その濃淡の印象は、フィルム写真における印画紙と像を焼き付けるランプの関係、そしてそれを光の濃淡として視覚化するフォトグラムを思わせる。デプスマップのグラデーションが奥行きに応じて濃淡を変えるように、フォトグラムもまた光の届く距離をグレースケールで示す。 もとよりAIによる画像生成は、デジタル写真よりもフィルム写真を現像する感覚に近い。透明の薬剤に白い印画紙を沈めると像が浮かび上がってくる、そうした暗室体験の再帰がある。画像生成は学習元の精査さえ可能ならば、写真表現を前向きに更新するメディアとなるだろう。 本シリーズは作家自らが都内で撮影した写真やデータを参照元に、それらと生成モデルが内部知識として持つ東京のイメージをかけ合わせて制作されたと思われる。その際、AIを用いて新規的なイメージを表現するのでなく、むしろフォトグラムやオプティカル合成といった既視感のある表現と、図像を強引にまとめるという現時点のAIの特徴を合わせることで、過去の蓄積を参照するという画像生成の方法論自体を浮かび上がらせる。それによって写真家がカメラを介して向き合う外界というものが、生成モデルが蓄える膨大な人々の痕跡やオンライン上の情報領域にまで拡張されたことを物語っている。 「“TOKYO”」展［筆者撮影］ 鑑賞日：2026/07/02（木）

items.album: 【京都】Co-program 2026 早川葉南子「遊戯─演習2─」

items.excerpt: スチル：Lisa Strozyk 京都芸術センターにて、公募プログラムCo-program2026 早川葉南子「遊戯─演習2─」が開催されます。 本展は、「見られる身体」とその主体性をテーマに、社会や他者の視線、歴史や制度によって形づくられる身体のあり方を問い直すダンス作品です。本作では、少女的な身体とダンサーの身体を重ね合わせながら、既存の規範や役割に回収されない「制御不能な身体」の可能性を探ります。 創作には、移民・移住経験をもつダンサーたちとの国際的なリサーチをもとに、京都・ベルリン・パリ・ニューヨークなど異なる文化的背景をもつアーティストが参加。ダンサーに余越保子、上田愛華、Kidows Kim、音楽に小松千倫とDoveを迎え、コスチュームデザインはLee Chang Hyunとの協働により制作します。 ＜早川葉南子＞ 現在、ベルリン、ブリュッセルを拠点に活動するダンスメーカー。多摩美術大学にて勅使川原三郎の指導を受ける。ブリュッセルのP.A.R.T.S.トレーニングサイクル（3年間のコンテンポラリーダンス教育プログラム）を修了。Tino Sehgal, Michiel Van

items.body: The ruins of Pompeii, Buffalo mozzarella from Caserta, the switchback drop of the Amalfi Coast, a sfogliatella still warm from the oven, just after a pizza. Now add thirty years of the Ariano Folkfestival to the list, because apparently once Campania gets good at something, it doesn’t stop. Set eight hundred metres up in the Apennine hills, the hilltop town of Ariano Irpino transforms every August into an open-air crossroads for global roots, brass traditions, and tropical sound systems. Celebrating its 30th edition under the banner of three decades of cultural resistance, the community-led gathering opens its main run tomorrow, Thursday 20 August, and blends international heritage with late-night electronic sessions across historic public spaces through Sunday. Locals call Ariano Irpino la città tricolle, the three-hill town, built along the old route traders once used to move between Naples and Puglia. For four days every August, the streets around it become the festival. Wander away from Piazzale Calvario and you’ll land at a tavolata popolare, one of the communal tables set up through town where Irpinia’s wine, cheese and cured-meat producers sell alongside the crowd rather than to it, with craft stalls of local pottery filling the gaps between. Mornings belong to Villa Comunale, where workshops and yoga sessions run under the castle walls before the day gets going; once the last band on the main stage finishes, Sonazone picks up the slack and keeps DJs playing into the early hours. Out at VolksCamp, the campsite in the Boschetto Pasteni woodland, the same thing happens on a smaller scale through the afternoon, its own stage running for whoever’s pitched a tent among the roughly 20,000 who came through last year. Thursday’s bill runs Caribbean into West African into North African. Kobo Town open with a full band built around Drew Gonsalves’ voice and cuatro: trombone-heavy horns, acoustic guitar and a calypso rhythm section carrying his lyrics, roots reggae basslines pushing under dub poetry delivery. Flammer Dance Band follow with seven players locked into interlocking funk grooves, guitar and bass trading rhythm lines under synth and saxophone leads, built on the 1970s West African records that shaped them. Retro Cassetta closes the night with no band at all, just Badreddine Haoutar behind two decks running actual cassette tapes, raï, chaâbi and gnawa recordings he’s spent years digging out of Morocco, Algeria and Libya, tape hiss and all, mixed live rather than sampled clean. Friday moves from the Alps to the Atlas. Faccianuvola, the Valtellina-born Alessandro Feruda, plays solo with laptop and synths, layering atmospheric electronic pads under heavily processed, autotuned vocals. Tasuta N-Imal take the stage as a full six-piece: lead guitar and rhythm guitar over the derbouka and djembé drums, the singer keeping time on a big dendoum drum and metal qraqeb castanets, the whole band performing in the traditional dress of Morocco’s Aït Aata tribe while singing in Amazigh. Fidju Kitxora closes the night as a single masked performer who keeps his face hidden throughout, working live vocal samples and field recordings into funaná and semba rhythms through a bank of synthesisers, part DJ set, part live performance. Saturday runs entirely on electronics, three different starting points. Kutu open as a full band: French violinist Théo Ceccaldi improvising over Ethiopian singers Hewan Gebrewold and Haleluya Tekletsadik, keyboards and drums pushing the Azmari vocal calls of Addis Ababa’s underground scene into trance territory. 64 Ksana follow as a trio, Jundo on synthesiser, Jaeyeon singing and playing Korean percussion she trained in through the Gyeonggi minyo folk tradition, Ejo on percussion with roots in dub, building techno beats around the ritual rhythms of Korean shamanic ceremony. Gregotechno close the night as a duo, Marc Vilajuana and Alejandro Narés, one voice singing live Gregorian chant over the other’s techno production, with video art projected behind them drawn from Romanesque church architecture. Sunday’s bill, the biggest of the four days, closes on two very different live formats. La Chiva Gantiva play as a full band, horns and guitars driving Afro-Colombian percussion through punk and rock energy at speed, the sound they named punkclore themselves. Martin Meissonnier closes it out behind the decks rather than on an instrument, a DJ set built from decades of the music he helped produce and collect, moving through Congolese rumba, Nigerian afrobeat and Caribbean sound systems in one continuous mix. Thirty years, one missed edition. In 2020, the Associazione Red Sox called off the festival because of Covid; every other August since 1996, they’ve put it on out of a hill town in the Apennines, funded by volunteers, the comune and the region, with musicians choosing a piazza in Irpinia over stages that pay more. This year’s programme runs under the line trent’anni di resistenza culturale, thirty years of cultural resistance, and Francesco Fodarella‘s team have earned the right to call it that.   Thirty years in the making. The Ariano Folkfestival opens tomorrow! Day tickets & full-run passes are still available now via the official festival page   https://rhythmpassport.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ariano-Folkfestival-arianofolkfestival-Instagram-reel.mp4 The post Event Preview: Ariano Folkfestival 30 (Ariano Irpino, Italy; Thursday 20th to Sunday 23rd August 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: “Berani” means “the exile”, and it follows someone who leaves home in search of freedom and a better future. Rabie Houti made that move himself, leaving Oran, the Algerian city where raï took shape, for Montpellier around 2014. “Berani” is the second single from his upcoming album, after “Rwahou“. A violinist and singer, Houti leads the Rabie Houti Band, drawn from Montpellier’s cross-cultural music scene. His Algerian violin, rooted in the Arab-Andalusian repertoire, leads a band that pitches it against electric blues guitar, drums, bass and synths. The EP that “Berani” trails leans harder into rock than his earlier records. He belongs to the sono mondiale lineage, the French world-music movement whose defining figure was Rachid Taha, the Algerian-French singer who drove raï and chaabi into rock. Stream “Berani” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Rabie Houti – Berani appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: It's rare to come back home empty-handed from a foray into Corbett vs Dempsey’s territorial waters, and this mission is no exception. Today, we're talking about the Atlantic Pact, set between the ever-erupting, volcanic Chicago scene and the anarcho-free stronghold of Amsterdam, that nothing and no one will ever conquer. No drones, tanks, Patriots, or F-35s, but the only weapons useful to humanity: reeds, pianos, drums, and basses. These Things Happen provide them with their sophomore album, "A Gentle Reminder", following their 2022 self-titled debut. This album, recorded at Hyde Park Jazz Festival in Chicago and at WNUR Studio, Northwestern University, confirms the band's recipe: original songs interspersed with renditions of Misha Mengelberg and Thelonious Monk, presented not in a slavish, calligraphic manner but through a contemporary reinterpretation of tradition. The players on the field deserve to be met up close. Keefe Jackson, tenor saxophone, bass clarinet. Born in Fayetteville, Arkansas, he arrived in Chicago in 2001 and performed across US and Europe with the likes of Tomeka Reid, Tim Days, Dave Rempis, Mike Reed, Jeb Bishop, Jason Adasiewicz, Satoko Fujii, Ab Baars and Bill Meyer. His partner in crime on the other side of the Pond, Oscar Jan Hoogland, piano, is a top notch badass. A leading figure on the Dutch impro scene, Hoogland sprung onto the Amsterdam landscape around 20 years ago, at the forefront of a new group of improvisers to arrive and simultaneously uphold the tradition of New Dutch Swing even while tearing it apart. As always, collaborations define the breadth of a musician's chromatic palette and so, read here about Oscar: improvisation with Senegalese singer Mola Sylla and percussionist Frank Rosaly; sound installations and performances with Practical Music and his Phonograph Orchestra; cumbia with Ibelisse Guardia Ferraguttis’s Superinca and the Galactic Green; Ethiopian jazz and Eritrean traditional music with Semer Welday’s Adulis. His work with Arnold de Boer and the duo with mythologic Han Bennink incontrovertibly attests to the caliber of the artist. The rhythm section that supports the two pals features Jason Roebke on double bass (collaborations with Ken Vandermark, Jeb Bishop, Jeff Parker, Chad Taylor, and Rob Mazurek), who replaced Joshua Abrams during the process, and Mikel Patrick Avery on drums (Rob Mazurek, Marshall Allen Tomeka Reid, Jeff Parker, and Kurt Vile on his CV). The record: Jackson's opening track "20 Years Past 12 O'Clock," a sonic excursus that moves across multiple time scales, is followed by a piece by Hoogland dedicated to Ab Baars, "Upperclass Underground," and a reinterpretation of Monk’s "Green Chimneys," whose genesis is described as follows: "it started out as a punk song on the setlist before taking a thin-threaded turn on the night." Two original compositions keep the pace in the right mood, constantly balancing compositional rigor with a loose flow, free from excessive constraints. The revisitation of Mengelberg's "Een Beetje Zenuwachtig," from minor to major, pays homage to the legendary Ukrainian pianist's key change when he played "Round Midnight" in Chicago, while "Well You Needn't" pushes Monk "max so far," as Hoogland puts it, with a sculptural declination of an ongoing sonic pendulum swinging between modernity and tradition. The album closes with “Over het Zijn en het Hoera”, its title drawn from an absurdist story by Dutch writer and artist Armando. As it has rightly been said, this is music that knows its history inside out and wears it lightly. The generosity of spirit here, between players, between cities, between Monk and Mengelberg, between composition and the moment, is the real subject. You know, sometimes things like these happen. items.excerpt: ブルガリアにおけるピアソラ演奏の第一人者として知られ、習得難度が非常に高いアルゼンチン式バンドネオンを本場最高水準と遜色ない超絶技巧で操る若き奇才ストヤン・カライヴァノフによるデビュー・アルバム。とにかく一音一音が明瞭。取り上げる楽曲はピアソラ曲やそれ以前のこてこてな古典ながら、哀愁や泣きを深く滲ませるより古典特有の過密と言っていい情感をぎゅっと凝縮しながら若さ溢れる疾走感とアタッキーなタッチで叩きつけてくる。楽曲自体も素晴らしいが、それ以上に彼が提示するバンドネオンの楽器としてのポテンシャルの高さに改めて驚かされる。圧倒的な構築性により複数の旋律が絡み合う立体的なサウンドは芸術。

items.body:
BURNOUT SYNDROMES are celebrating a decade since their major debut by returning to where it all began.

On 19 August, the Japanese rock trio released Haikyu!! BOS - Syudaikatachinoutage -, a special cover album dedicated to the beloved anime Haikyu!!. Translating to “Banquet of Theme Songs,” the record sees the band revisiting the music that has soundtracked the series through their own interpretations.

BURNOUT SYNDROMES' history with Haikyu!! stretches back to their 2016 major-label debut, when 'FLY HIGH!!' was selected as an opening theme for the anime's second season. They later returned with 'hikariare' and 'PHOENIX', further cementing the series as a defining part of the band's musical journey.

For their 10th anniversary, the Osaka trio have turned the spotlight on the wider Haikyu!! soundtrack. The 12-track album features their takes on songs originally performed by SPYAIR, NICO Touches the Walls, Sukima Switch, tacica, CHiCO with HoneyWorks, and SUPER BEAVER, alongside BURNOUT SYNDROMES' own Haikyu!! themes.

The album artwork also features specially drawn illustrations from Haikyu!!, bringing the worlds of the band and the anime together once more. Coinciding with the release, a JUMP MV for 'PHOENIX' featuring illustrations from Haruichi Furudate's Haikyu!! manga premiered today.

BURNOUT SYNDROMES are also headed to the Philippines next month. The band will perform at BURNOUT SYNDROMES LIVE IN MANILA 2026 on 5 September at The Crossroad Center, with the show scheduled to begin at 6 PM. Get tickets here.

items.body:
Slowspin Combines Ambient-Jazz & Hindustani Folk On New Album 'AFTERIMAGE'

19 August 2026

'Afterimage', the latest album by Zeerak Ahmed aka SLOWSPIN, isn't the first time the U.S.-based Karachi-rooted artist has expressed the inner worlds of the diaspora. Her archival sound installation 'Mother, I Am Compelled to Leave' has done that before. Neither is it the first time she has combined folk influences with contemporary instrumentation. That's been done with similar themes on her previous critically lauded album 'TALISMAN'.

However, the new 10-track record sees her grip the universality in both aspects tighter and shed off the excess further with a minimalist approach. The blunt, heavy hits of drums with brushes or mallets, clean guitar strums, and sometimes harps and woodwinds too, put the work in the textural jazz palette along with its slightly improvisational nature. The simple melodies on tracks like lullaby-like 'Jaat Rahi' or the sustained longings of 'Hari Hari' add a safe consonance to the album, while a track like 'Mausam / Broken Hearted One' layers its melodies till its shapes obscure into a bed. All of these instances give 'AFTERIMAGE' an ambient effect but with a dynamic character, creating a standout lexicon for the album that is truly its crown jewel.

Meanwhile, the influence of the folk canon, no doubt informed by Ahmed's academic and curatorial work on South Asian female folk musical traditions, opens up the themes of the album from just the diaspora experience to anyone who has had to move away from loved ones, said emotional goodbyes, felt the need for them and longed for the life before them at the same time.

The English-language songwriting on the album does add variation to the album, but they don't share the perfect marriage with the placating soft instrumentation and the focused sentimentality of the patient melodic expression on a single word that the Braj, Hindustani and Urdu counterparts feature. It's the latter world where 'AFTERIMAGE' functions best, creating a sonic world where it can take flight into shoegazy crescendos like on 'Mother I Have To Leave' or stay convinced in a memorable, delicate performance as in 'Jaat Rahi'.

Listen to 'Afterimage' below and follow Slowspin for more information.

Image: Slowspin & executive producer, bassist and synth player Shahzad Ismaily by Tonje Thileson

items.body: Water will always follow the path of least resistance, trickling along and naturally finding the easiest course. It does so effortlessly, without thought. Of course, life is rarely like that…but somehow, things usually have a way of working out for the best. Relationships may turn to ash and dreams may be broken, but life has a way of (eventually) settling down. Glorious things await, and they wouldn’t have been possible without heartache or pain. Even at the lowest ebb, there is always hope, and accelerated growth is possible after experiencing pain. From ground level, what looks messy and blinded by fog can look crystal clear from a bird’s-eye view. Battle-worn, the heart can recover and be all the stronger for its experience. The pandemic has been a ripe blossom for creativity, even at a time when the rest of the world experienced stagnation, confinement, and death. In 2020, music, creativity, and the arts in general all grew with the advent of lockdowns and the absence of light. Matt Robertson’s ‘Enveleau’ (Subtempo, April 30) finds envelopment, peace, and ultimately gratitude in and among its surroundings, be it in the solitude of lockdown or out in the open. No matter where you are, you can be thankful for where you’ve been planted. Robertson’s ambient sound and subtle, flexible electronics combine with organic techno to produce radiant and effervescent music. It’s benefitted from being in and enjoying its own surroundings; you get the feeling that Robertson loved every minute of creation and recording, pouring it all into every tweak and tonal transmutation. Rhythms are crisp, lean, and in great shape, but there are also jaw-dropping ambient vistas to gaze upon, such as the sublime ‘Syntropic’, which features glowing sunset synths and a glorious, expanding atmosphere. The music doesn’t have to work hard to make things happen; it naturally follows the path of least resistance. It should be like that with the right person, too. You won’t have to work so hard to be happy when you find them. It will just happen. Like Enveleau, life is smoother when you go with the flow. www.subtempo.com
